The refusals, all before any effect: `unknown_slot`; `not_installed`, naming the resolved version and the exact `vibe install -g PACKAGE@VER` that would supply it; and `selection_required` when a requirement matches several installed versions and nothing narrows it. `vibe app exec` neither installs nor changes any default, state or file — that is the whole distinction from `vibe app use` — and it is distinct from the existing `vibe app run PACKAGE LAUNCHER`, which runs one declared launcher of one installation.

p.MIGRATION-DECLARATION: **Decided 2026-11-10 — the declaration and the inputs.** `[[application.migration]]` rows carry `id` (a stable token), `name` (human), optional `description`, `default` (boolean, whether an attended offer preselects it), and the two tables `export` and `import`. **Each of the two is exactly one step declaration of the existing `StepDecl` grammar restricted to the kinds `recipe` and `shell`** (PROP-065 `#kinds`), with `kind` required: an `env`, `archive`, `sources`, `native`, `copy` or `agent` migration step is a validation refusal naming the kind, because a migration moves user state and must not install, download or delegate. Both run through the ordinary engine — the step runner, the interpreters, `needs`, the display panel of PROP-065 `#display`, the cancellation of `#cancellation` and the run records of `#runs` — which is what MIGRATION's "executed as ordinary recipe steps" names. **The inputs**, as environment variables beside the ones PROP-065 `#templates` already passes: `VIBE_MIGRATION_ID`; `VIBE_MIGRATION_WORK`, the shared work directory `<home>/cache/app-migrate/<slot>/<from>-to-<to>/<timestamp>/`, which the export writes into and the import reads from; `VIBE_FROM_APP_ROOT` and `VIBE_FROM_VERSION`; `VIBE_TO_APP_ROOT` and `VIBE_TO_VERSION`; and the usual `VIBE_PACKAGE`, `VIBE_PLATFORM`, `VIBE_ARCH`. `VIBE_PACKAGE` is the package tree of the version that owns the step — the old version's for the export, the new version's for the import — so each side runs its own package's script, which is what lets a template change a migration between versions. The export's PATH leads with the **old** installation's payload and proxy directories and the import's with the **new** one's, built by the same `StepPaths::child_env` a step requirement uses, so `npm ls -g` in the export is the old npm and `npm install -g` in the import is the new one without either script knowing a version number. `VIBE_OUT` is **not** set and `$out` is not expandable: a migration produces no payload. The template-level consequence is that a Node template declares its migration once and every produced version has it.

p.MIGRATION-FAILURE: **Decided 2026-11-10 — consent, and the failure semantics the owner stated.** `vibe app migrate SLOT FROM TO [--only ID]… [--all] [--yes] [--resume] [--json]`. Entries are independent and run in declaration order; `--only` selects, `--all` takes every declared entry, and with neither an attended terminal offers the entries with the `default` ones preselected while an unattended run without `--yes` refuses with `consent_required` and prints the exact command — the "offered, never run without consent" of MIGRATION. `install -g` / `update -g` that gives a slot a new version, and `vibe app use` that moves its default, make the same offer attended and print the same command unattended; neither ever migrates on its own. **Failure**: an `export` that fails stops **that entry** before its import runs, changes nothing, and is recorded `export_failed`; because the export runs first, a failed export can never leave a half-migrated new version. An `import` that fails **leaves the new version installed and the slot's default exactly where the user put it**, never rolls back, never uninstalls and never re-runs the export; the entry is recorded `import_failed` with the step, the work directory and the log path. One entry's failure does not stop the others. The work directory is **always kept**, success or failure, because it is the evidence of what was and was not carried, and `vibe app work` lists and cleans it like any other. The report — human and `vibe-app-migration/1` (`schemas/application_migration.jtd.json`) — names, per entry, the outcome, and for a failure **what was not carried**: the entry's `name`, the step that failed, its log path, the work directory, and the exact `vibe app migrate SLOT FROM TO --only ID --resume` that retries it; `--resume` reuses the kept work directory and re-runs only the import when the export already succeeded, the same resume contract PROP-065 `#resume` gives an installation. The command exits 0 when every selected entry succeeded, 1 when any failed. The migration outcomes are recorded with the **new** installation so a later `vibe app list --json` and a later migration can see what already moved.

p.VERSION-FILE-KEYED: **Decided 2026-11-10 on the owner's generalisation requirement — the third version-file format, which is what a Java pass needs.** `#VERSION-FILE-FORMATS` closed the set at `plain` and `tool-versions`, both of which answer for one tool per file or for asdf's own file. sdkman's `.sdkmanrc` holds **several** tools in one file (`java=21.0.4-tem`, `maven=3.9.9`), as asdf's `.tool-versions` and `mise.toml` do, so the general shape — a file of `key`/`version` pairs in which each slot edits only its own line — is declared once, as `format = "keyed"`, and not once per tool. A `keyed` row carries `names` (an ordered array of file names, as `plain` does), `key` (this package's key in the file: `java`, `nodejs`), and the **line syntax, declared from a closed vocabulary and never as a pattern**: `separator` is one of `"equals"` (`key=value`, `.sdkmanrc`), `"whitespace"` (`key value…`, `.tool-versions`) or `"colon"` (`key: value`), with no default — an author states it; `comment` is `"hash"` (the default), `"semicolon"` or `"none"`; and `extra`, for a line that carries more than one value after the key, is `"first"` (take the first, report the rest unused — asdf's rule) or `"refuse"` (the default: a second value on the key's line is a reported, unusable line, which is what `java=21.0.4-tem extra` should be). Nothing else is declarable: no regular expression, no section headers, no quoting modes, no multi-line values, because `#TEMPLATE-SOURCE-KINDS` and PROP-065 `#principle` forbid an expression language in a declaration and the three separators cover every file the 17-tool survey found. **`tool-versions` becomes the short spelling of exactly one `keyed` row** — `separator = "whitespace"`, `comment = "hash"`, `extra = "first"` — so there is one reader and one writer and the format set grows by one, not two; the old spelling keeps working byte-for-byte and the two can never drift, because the sugar is expanded before anything reads a file. **A keyed file is read exactly as `#VERSION-FILE-FORMATS` prescribes for any version file** and joins the same precedence, with two rules the shape forces: a line whose key is not this package's is **ignored and not reported**, because another slot's key in a shared file is not a defect, and a key the home has no installed package for is likewise ignored — a `.sdkmanrc` naming `maven` on a machine with no maven package must not make the file unusable for `java`. The value is a version requirement or a channel name, as `plain`'s line is. **One file may therefore resolve several slots at once**, each from its own key, which is the whole reason the format exists.

p.VERSION-FILE-WRITE: **Decided 2026-11-10, amended 2026-11-11 — `--write-version-file`, for both formats, which is nvm's `--save` / `-w`.** A flag on `vibe app use`, on `vibe install -g` of an application, and on `vibe app env`: `--write-version-file[=PATH]`. **On `vibe app env` it is nvm's `use --save` exactly** — it changes the shell and the file and **not** the slot's global default, which is the one thing `vibe app use` could not do and the reason this third home exists. Because `vibe app env` resolves several slots in one call, *which* slot's file is written is **said and never guessed**: the flag needs exactly one `--use SLOT=VER`, and every other shape is a usage refusal naming the flag — no `--use` at all (name the version with one), more than one (run it once per slot), `--unset` (there is nothing to record), `--use SLOT=none` (the slot is off for this shell), and a `--use` that resolved to no installed version (the slot's state, with the install command when there is one). The written file is reported on **stderr**, because `vibe app env`'s stdout carries the lines a shell evaluates and nothing else, and `--json` carries it as `versionFile` of `vibe-app-env/1` (`AV-FMT-106`). It writes the **resolved** version — never the requirement or the channel the user typed, because a version file that says `lts` tells the next reader nothing about what was chosen — into the slot's declared version file. **Which file.** Without a value: the nearest file the `#VERSION-FILE-FORMATS` search already found, in the directory it was found in, so `--save` edits the file the project is actually using; with no such file, the **first** `names` entry of the **first** declared row, created in the project root when inside a project and in the working directory otherwise. With a value: exactly that path, whose format is decided by matching its file name against the declared `names` of every row — a path matching none is a refusal naming the path and the names the package declares, never a guess at a format. **How each format is written.** `plain` writes the one line and nothing else, keeping a trailing newline. `keyed` is an **in-place edit of one line**: every other line of the file — other keys, comments, blank lines, unknown content, the file's own line endings — is preserved byte-for-byte, the key's line is rewritten in the file's own declared separator with the spacing it already had, and a key the file does not carry is appended as the last line; an absent file is created holding that one line. That is the rule the whole format exists for, and it is what makes two slots able to write one `.sdkmanrc` without either destroying the other's answer. **Refusals, all before any write**: a path that is a symbolic link, naming it (vibe never writes through a link it did not make); a slot whose package declares no version file at all, naming the slot and the package; a `keyed` file in which the key's line appears twice, naming both line numbers, because an editor that guesses which duplicate to keep would silently discard a declaration. The written file is reported by path with the version written, and `--json` carries both.

p.ECOSYSTEM-ADAPTER: **Owner decision 2026-11-10 — the ecosystem adapter: one declaration by which a runtime package installs, lists, removes and self-upgrades the packages of its *own* ecosystem, and which vibe core understands without knowing one ecosystem word.** Almost every runtime carries its own package manager — npm in Node, pip in Python, rubygems in Ruby, cargo and rustup components in Rust — and every version manager surveyed has the same three needs over it: install a list of ecosystem packages into a newly installed runtime version, observe what is installed in one version, and upgrade the bundled manager itself. Java has none of this and declares no adapter, which is the test that the mechanism is optional. **The declaration.** `[[application.ecosystem]]` rows, each with `id` (a stable token, **opaque to vibe** — `npm`, `pip`, `gems`, `cargo`, `rustup-component`; vibe never interprets it and only ever echoes it), `name` (human), optional `description`, and up to four verbs: `install` (required), `list`, `remove` and `self_upgrade`. **Several adapters per package are admitted** — a Rust package declares `rustup-component` and `cargo` — and each is addressed by its `id`; two rows with one `id` are a validation refusal naming the TOML path, as is a row whose `id` is not a token. **Each verb is exactly one step declaration** of the existing `StepDecl` grammar restricted to the kinds `recipe` and `shell`, with `kind` required — the same restriction and the same reason `#MIGRATION-DECLARATION` gives: an adapter runs a command inside an installed runtime and must not install, download, delegate or change the user's environment, so an `env`, `archive`, `sources`, `native`, `copy` or `agent` adapter step is a refusal naming the kind. Both run through the ordinary engine — the step runner, the interpreters, `needs`, the display of PROP-065 `#display`, the cancellation of `#cancellation` — so the adapter introduces no second execution path. **Where a verb runs.** In the context of the one installation it configures: PATH leads with that installation's payload and proxy directories, built by the same `StepPaths::child_env` a migration's import side uses, so `npm` is *that version's* npm and no script knows a version number; `VIBE_PACKAGE` is that version's package tree; the working directory is the run's own work directory `<home>/cache/app-ecosystem/<slot>/<version>/<timestamp>/`, kept on failure and on success as a migration's is, listed and cleaned by `vibe app work`. `VIBE_OUT` is not set and `$out` is not expandable: an adapter produces no payload. **The item list, and the injection rule, which is a law and not a style note.** Item strings are **opaque**: vibe never parses, splits, quotes, escapes, validates or reorders them — `@scope/pkg@^1.2`, `typescript`, `pnpm@9`, a git URL and a local path are all one item each, exactly as the user or the author wrote them. They are handed to the `install` and `remove` verbs **as separate argv elements appended to the step's own argv, and are never interpolated into a command string**. The structural consequence, which is what makes the rule checkable rather than hopeful: `install` and `remove` **must declare `kind = "recipe"`**, because a `recipe` step is a script invoked with arguments and a `shell` step is an authored command *string* into which a list could only be spliced; a `shell` `install` or `remove` is a validation refusal naming the field and the reason. The script reads the items as `"$@"`; for a script that prefers reading them, the same list is also passed as `VIBE_ECOSYSTEM_ITEMS` (one item per line) with `VIBE_ECOSYSTEM_ITEM_COUNT`, and `VIBE_ECOSYSTEM_ID` names the adapter. `list` and `self_upgrade` take no items and may be either kind. **The `list` verb's answer is a file, not stdout.** The step writes one item per line into the file named by `VIBE_ECOSYSTEM_LIST` in its work directory; vibe reads it, trims each line, drops the empty ones, and treats what is left as opaque items — so no ecosystem's listing format is ever parsed, the answer survives a manager that writes notices to stdout, and the step's own output stays what it is, a log. A declared `list` whose file is absent or empty is an empty list and is reported as such, never an error. **The record.** Each run writes `<work>/ecosystem.json` (`vibe-app-ecosystem/1`) with the adapter id, the verb, the items asked for, the outcome and the per-verb log path, and the installation record retains, per adapter, the last applied list and the last observed list with their times — so `vibe app describe` answers what a version carries without running anything, which is what makes an observation cheap enough to report.

p.ECOSYSTEM-RECOMMENDS: **Owner decision 2026-11-10 — an author's recommended ecosystem items are PROP-065 features, and nothing new.** Three layers must stay distinct, and the owner named them: `[recommends]` is **vibe packages**, resolved by vibe (PROP-077 `#APP-RECOMMENDS`, the general package model); an author's recommended **ecosystem items** (Node suggesting `corepack` or `pnpm`, which are npm packages and not vibe packages) is this fact; and the user's own list is `#SLOT-EXTRAS`. The second and third differ only in who wrote the list and share one mechanism from the adapter down. **The declaration.** `[[application.ecosystem.recommends]]` rows, each with `ecosystem` (an `id` the package declares — an unknown id is a refusal naming it), `id` (a stable token, the row's own name), `item` (the opaque item string), `default` (boolean) and optional `name` / `reason`. **Each row is shorthand for one feature.** It synthesises an `[[installer_options.features]]` row with that `id`, that `default`, the row's `name` or its `item` as the name and its `reason` as the description, in **every** installer option of the package — because the recommendation is a property of the package and not of one platform's archive — and the item is added to the adapter's list exactly when that feature is in the chosen set. So everything PROP-065 `#features`, `#feature-tree` and `#profiles` already give applies with no new vocabulary: `--feature ID` / `--no-feature ID` turn one recommendation on or off, an attended terminal offers them in the same multi-select as every other feature, a declared profile may name them, the chosen set is **recorded with the installation** and reused by `update` unless named again, and a condition on a step may read one. An `id` that collides with an authored feature of any option is a validation refusal naming both TOML paths; the reserved shape is that an author who wants a tree, a requirement or an exclusive group writes the feature rows themselves and refers to the item with a recommends row of the same `id`, which is admitted and is the one way the two spellings meet. **Why a shorthand at all, rather than making authors write the feature and a mapping**: the row is the mapping, one line instead of two declarations that can disagree, and it keeps the item string — the only part vibe must never parse — in exactly one place.

p.SLOT-EXTRAS: **Owner decision 2026-11-10 — the user's own per-slot, per-ecosystem list, and what is applied after an install.** This is nvm's `$NVM_DIR/default-packages` generalised: not "default npm packages" but "what this user wants in every new version of this slot's runtime, in that runtime's own ecosystem". **The declaration is the user's, in their own settings** (`~/.vibe/config.toml`): `[slot.<slot>.extras.<ecosystem>]` with `add` (an array of opaque items) and `drop` (an array of **recommendation ids**, not items — dropping is opting out of a named author recommendation, and naming an id rather than re-typing an item is what keeps the two sides from drifting). An unknown slot, an unknown ecosystem id or an unknown recommendation id in the settings is **reported once and otherwise ignored**, never an error: a user's settings file outlives the packages it mentions, and refusing an install over a stale line in a file the user wrote by hand would be the wrong trade. **The final list, computed per ecosystem, in this order**: the items of the author recommendations that are in the installation's chosen feature set, in declaration order; minus every recommendation the user dropped; plus the user's `add` items, in their own order; de-duplicated by exact string, first occurrence winning. That list is handed to the adapter's `install` verb as `#ECOSYSTEM-ADAPTER` prescribes. **When.** After `install -g` or `update -g` has placed a **new version** of a slot and written its record — never before, because a half-installed runtime cannot run its own package manager — and once per declared adapter with a non-empty list. Not on a reinstall of a version already installed, not on `vibe app use`, and never on a resolution, a listing or a prompt hook. **Two flags, and they are not the same flag.** `--no-recommends` skips the **author's** recommendations of both kinds — the vibe packages of PROP-077 `#APP-RECOMMENDS` and the ecosystem items of `#ECOSYSTEM-RECOMMENDS` — because an author's recommendation is one idea with two spellings and a user who declines it declines both; `--no-extras` skips the **user's own** `add` list. A `drop` is honoured in every case, including under `--no-extras`: a flag that says "do not install my extras" must never cause **more** to be installed than the user asked for, and treating a withdrawal of consent as part of the skipped list would do exactly that. With both flags, or with an empty final list, the adapter is not run at all. **Failure never touches the runtime.** A failing `install` verb leaves the new version installed, its slot default exactly where the user put it, and the installation record written: the failure is reported as a warning with the adapter id, the items asked for, the step, its log path and the exact retry command `vibe app extras apply <slot>`, and it is recorded in the installation's adapter record so a later `vibe app describe` still says what was not carried. It never rolls back, never uninstalls and never changes the exit status of a successful install — an extra is an extra. **The visible surface** is one command family, named after the user-facing concept while the declaration is named after the mechanism: `vibe app extras list SLOT [--ecosystem ID] [--json]` (what the final list is, and what the adapter's `list` observes in the installed version), `apply SLOT` (compute and install it now, the retry), `add ITEM…` / `drop ID…` (edit the user's own settings), `remove SLOT ITEM…` (the adapter's `remove` verb — uninstalling an item, which is not the same act as dropping it from a list), `self-upgrade SLOT [--ecosystem ID]` (the adapter's `self_upgrade`), and `import SLOT FILE [--ecosystem ID]`, which reads one item per line from a file, `#` comments and blank lines ignored, and appends them to the user's `add` — the whole content of `$NVM_DIR/default-packages`, and cheap enough to include because the format it reads is the format `#ECOSYSTEM-ADAPTER`'s `list` already writes. `self-upgrade` sits in this family rather than in one of its own because it is the fourth verb of the same adapter and a second command family for one verb is not worth its weight. **Out of scope, named so nobody assumes it**: a project-level extras list (`vibe.toml` saying what a project wants in a runtime) is a different question — it would need a project's consent model and a project-scoped record — and is not opened here.

p.PACKAGE-ACTIONS: **Decided 2026-11-10 — the general "package action" verb is deliberately NOT built, and this fact records why, because the design proposed it and the owner asked for the question to be re-answered.** The proposal was a visible verb `vibe app action SLOT ID [VERSION]` over package-declared maintenance entries, generalising nvm's `--latest-npm` and `install-latest-npm`, listed by `vibe app describe` and built either on the existing `[[application.migration]]` mechanism with `FROM == TO` or on a dedicated declaration. It is dropped, and the reason is that it has **no consumer left**. Every maintenance act the 17-tool survey found is one of the four verbs of `#ECOSYSTEM-ADAPTER`: `nvm --latest-npm` / `install-latest-npm`, `pip install -U pip` and `gem update --system` are `self_upgrade`; `nvm --reinstall-packages-from` is `list` then `install` (`#ECOSYSTEM-MIGRATION`); `corepack` is an **item** of the npm adapter, not an act of its own; and `nvm install --skip-default-packages` / `default-packages` are `#SLOT-EXTRAS`. A general verb over a general declaration would therefore be a second spelling for the same four acts, which is exactly the "third parallel mechanism" the owner's own rule forbids. **Two things are kept from the proposal's analysis.** (1) The mechanism it would have been built on was right and is used: an adapter verb *is* one `StepDecl` run through the ordinary engine, and `FROM == TO` on a migration *is* admitted and tested (`crates/vibe-app/src/migrate.rs`), which is why `#ECOSYSTEM-MIGRATION` costs nothing. (2) Building it on `[[application.migration]]` would have been **wrong** for one concrete reason worth recording, because it is not obvious: the post-install offer is `migration_offer`, which finds the version to carry *from* — the newest other version in the slot — and answers nothing when there is none, so a maintenance entry expressed as a migration could never run after the **first** install of a runtime, which is precisely when `--latest-npm` is asked for. If a maintenance act outside the four verbs is ever found, it is a fifth adapter verb or a new declaration decided then, and the step grammar is already the carrier.

p.ECOSYSTEM-MIGRATION: **Decided 2026-11-10 — the npm-globals migration becomes the general case of the adapter, and the shim's two maintenance verbs become `self_upgrade`.** An adapter that declares both `list` and `install` already *is* the strategy `#MIGRATION` describes — observe in the old version, re-install in the new — so vibe **synthesises** one `[[application.migration]]`-shaped entry per such adapter instead of asking the package to write the same two scripts twice. The synthesised entry's id is `ecosystem:<adapter id>`; its `name` is the adapter's; its export is the adapter's `list` verb run by the **old** version, writing the observed items into the shared work directory; its import is the adapter's `install` verb run by the **new** version with exactly those items as its argv list; and its `default` is `true`, so an attended offer preselects it and an unattended run still needs `--yes`, which is `#MIGRATION-FAILURE`'s contract unchanged. The id prefix `ecosystem:` is **reserved**: an authored `[[application.migration]]` id in that namespace is a validation refusal naming the path, so a synthesised entry can never be shadowed. An adapter may set `migration = false` to suppress the synthesis, for a runtime whose ecosystem state should not travel between versions. Consequences, which are the point: `org.vibevm.node/node` declares **one** npm adapter and drops its hand-written `npm-globals` migration entry, the two nvm verbs `--reinstall-packages-from=<v>` / `--copy-packages-from=<v>` and `nvm reinstall-packages <v>` / `copy-packages <v>` map to `vibe app migrate node <v> <new> --only ecosystem:npm`, `nvm install --latest-npm` and `nvm install-latest-npm` map to `vibe app extras self-upgrade node --ecosystem npm`, and the differential suite's `globals` observation has a vibe-side answer (`vibe app extras list node --json`) as well as the `npm ls -g` it runs in both sandboxes — the suite keeps running the identical command in both, because an observation compared field by field must not differ in how it was taken. **The failure semantics are `#MIGRATION-FAILURE`'s, unchanged**: a failed export carries nothing and changes nothing, a failed import leaves the new version installed and the default where the user put it, the work directory is always kept, and nothing is ever rolled back.

p.VERSIONS-SELECT: **Decided 2026-11-12 on the owner's request, and the default is deliberately unchanged.** The owner's words were «положить сделать опцией: новейшая, предпочитать дроп, обрезать список. Сейчас пусть будет новейшая.» and, on the site layer, «пусть по-умолчанию в корпоративной поставке будет prefer-drop». **The problem.** In a closed network the version domain comes from a mirrored template snapshot and the payloads come from an `[artifacts] packages` drop a person filled by hand, and the two do not have to agree: the snapshot lists `22.23.5` because upstream published it, the drop holds `22.23.4` because that is the archive somebody carried in, and `vibe install -g node@22` — or `nvm install 22`, which calls it — resolves to a version whose bytes are nowhere on the machine and fails with no network to fall back on. **The setting.** `~/.vibe/config.toml` gains `[versions] select = "newest" | "prefer-drop" | "drop-only"`, kebab-case spellings read in any letter case. `newest` (the **built-in default**) is today's behaviour and nvm's own rule: the newest version satisfying the requirement, whatever this machine holds — an open network must not change behaviour because a closed one needs another rule. `prefer-drop` picks the newest **available** version the requirement admits and falls back to `newest` when none is available, so a drop that has not been filled yet still gets the ordinary refusal about the missing file rather than a second one about policy. `drop-only` admits only available versions and otherwise refuses, naming the version `newest` would have picked and the exact path its payload belongs at (`vibe artifacts where` prints every file and digest). **Available** means exactly two things, which are the same fact seen twice: the drop already holds every input the installer option this platform would select downloads — the `in drop` mark of `#VERSIONS-LIST-OUTPUT`, computed by **that** probe and no other, so the listing and the policy can never disagree — **or** the version is installed in this home already, which downloads nothing at all and would otherwise be re-downloaded by the very policy meant to avoid downloads. The one-line note names which of the two applied — `(in drop; …)` or `(installed; …)` — because announcing an installed version as «in drop» would be a sentence about a file that is not there. **Where it applies, and where it does not.** Wherever a requirement is resolved to a version of an application package: `install -g`, `update -g`, `app plan`, a version file whose value is partial (`#VERSION-FILE-VALUE`), `describe`, `migrate`, the portable surfaces, every `requires` entry of PROP-065 `#app-dependencies`, and therefore nvm. `app use` and `app env --use` need nothing done to them and get nothing: they choose among the versions this home has **installed**, where every candidate is available by the definition above, so no policy can move their answer. It is applied by **narrowing the requirement to an exact pin before the registries resolve it**, at the one resolution chokepoint, exactly as `#CHANNEL-SYNTAX` lowers a channel — no registry and no caller knows the policy exists, and `newest` returns before a domain is read, a drop is listed or the index is opened. A channel requirement is narrowed within its own members. An **exact** requirement (`=X.Y.Z`) is never redirected by any policy: a person who named one version meant that version, and under `drop-only` it resolves as before and refuses at the fetch, where the digest is known and the refusal can name the file. `vibe outdated` keeps reporting the **newest** version under every policy — what is newer upstream is a fact about upstream, not about this drop. `vibe artifacts where` is likewise exempt by construction: its whole job is to say where a payload belongs, and under `drop-only` that is precisely the payload the drop does not have yet. **Layering.** The ladder every other user-config value walks (PROP-019 `#site-profile` `##SITE-PROFILE-LAYER`): `VIBE_VERSIONS_SELECT` in the environment, then `[versions] select` in the user's own `config.toml`, then the applied site profile's `[versions]`, then the built-in `newest`. It is a per-key fallback by absence, not an `|=` like `[net] offline`: the three policies are not ordered by strictness in a way a merge could pick from. A corporate profile therefore carries `[versions] select = "prefer-drop"` once for every developer who applies it, and a developer still overrides it on their own machine. A misspelled policy **refuses** rather than falling through to `newest`, because a value that silently restored the default is the one failure a closed network cannot afford to debug. `vibe show config` and `vibe self apply --show` / `--dry-run` print the effective value with the layer that decided it (`env`, `config.toml`, `site profile`, `default`); `vibe app versions` says it in its trailer. **With no drop configured at all:** `prefer-drop` is `newest` (there is nothing to prefer) and `drop-only` refuses by naming the `[artifacts] packages` key to write — it cannot honour "only what the drop holds" when there is no drop. **Under `drop-only` the listing is not filtered**: `vibe app versions` shows the whole domain and says in its trailer that only an `in drop` or installed row is selectable, because hiding the unselectable rows would also hide the version an operator has to carry in, which is the one thing the refusal goes out of its way to name; `--in-drop` is the flag that narrows.

nvm.title: 5. The nvm replacement proof

p.VIBENVM: Owner request 2026-11-09: a standalone package `org.vibevm.node/vibenvm` provides an nvm-compatible command surface on top of sections 2–4, modelled on nvm-sh (the POSIX shell nvm, the richer one; not nvm-windows). Like nvm-sh it is sourced into the shell and defines an `nvm` function, because `nvm use` changes the current shell; the function maps every nvm command and flag onto vibe commands (`vibe app env`, `app use`, `app versions`, `app exec`, `app migrate`, `install -g`, `uninstall -g`, the slot off-switch) and holds no version logic of its own. Anything it cannot map is a gap in vibe's general machinery, not something to patch inside the shim.

p.VIBENVM-ALGORITHMIC-PROOF: Owner rule 2026-11-09: that vibe is a complete nvm replacement is proven algorithmically, never by an LLM's judgement or review. A differential conformance suite runs the same command sequences, request for request, against a pinned upstream nvm-sh release and against `vibenvm`, each in its own isolated home and shell, from the same starting state and the same local mirror of Node release files (no internet), and compares the observable results after every step: exit status, `node -v` / `npm -v`, the resolved `command -v node`, the PATH entries the tool owns, the installed-version list, the default and aliases, and the global npm packages of each version. Output text is compared only through declared, mechanical normalisations (paths, colours, timing). The command and flag inventory is extracted mechanically from the pinned nvm-sh itself (its `nvm --help` and the subcommand dispatch in `nvm.sh`), and nvm-sh's own test suite is reused where it runs offline. The gate passes only when every extracted command and flag has a passing differential case or appears on an explicit exclusion list that the owner has approved with a reason per entry. The suite is a committed, rerunnable script whose verdict is its exit code.

p.VIBENVM-PIN: **Decided 2026-11-10 — the pin, and why the pin and not the prose is authoritative.** The suite pins nvm-sh **v0.41.0**, annotated tag object `43d410caa64ba7928cef750e31fccbf5790c210c` at commit `4e8758a801eea9479b32a904f31093e410ddaba4`, the highest semantic-version tag on 2026-11-10. The inventory in `#VIBENVM-MAPPING` below was extracted mechanically from that tree (the dispatch `case` of the `nvm()` function, `nvm.sh` lines 4875–6742, and the inline help block at lines 4741–4858) and is recorded here as the design input, **not** as the gate: the gate re-extracts the inventory from whatever tag the suite pins at the time it runs, so a later nvm release neither invalidates this document nor can pass unnoticed — a command or flag the re-extraction finds and no case covers fails the coverage gate. That is also why the pin is one line in the suite's configuration and not a sentence of prose. Note for whoever reads the table: v0.41.0 carries surfaces the 0.40.x line did not — the version-category system (`--only=alpha|lts|non-lts|iojs` on nearly every verb, `$NVM_ONLY`), `install --offline`, `install/use --save|-w`, per-version install locks and `$NVM_AUTH_HEADER` — and they are in the table because they are in the pinned tree.

p.VIBENVM-MAPPING: **Decided 2026-11-10 — the command-by-command mapping.** Every subcommand of the pinned dispatch, with its flags, marked `maps` (expressible on the vibe surface of sections 2–4 as designed), `needs` (needs a named new vibe feature, which is then a deliverable of this task, never a patch inside the shim — VIBENVM's own rule), or `exclude` (a proposed exclusion with its reason, which only the owner can approve, `#VIBENVM-EXCLUSIONS`). The slot is `node`; `PKG` is `org.vibevm.node/node`.

Every `exclude` row above is owner-approved, one by one, on 2026-11-10 with the reason it carries, and only those twelve rows: #VIBENVM-EXCLUSIONS-APPROVED. The two default-packages rows the design proposed for exclusion were rejected by the owner and are now `maps`, through the general slot-extras feature.

p.VIBENVM-ARGUMENT-ORDER: **Decided 2026-11-11, after `nvm use 22 --save` was found exiting 0 and writing nothing.** `#VIBENVM-MAPPING` maps a subcommand's flags; it did not say **where a flag may stand**, and that is part of the surface a user learned rather than an implementation detail. nvm does not read one argument list: it reads a different one per branch, and the shim takes each branch's rule from the pinned `nvm.sh` v0.41.0 rather than inventing a uniform one. `install` reads **two passes** — the flags that select *which* version is installed (`-s`, `-b`, `-j`, `--offline`, `--lts`) must precede it, the flags that act *on* it (`--save` / `-w`, `--default`, `--latest-npm`, `--skip-default-packages`, `--no-progress`, `--reinstall-packages-from=` / `--copy-packages-from=`) may follow it, and one written on the wrong side of the version is nvm's own **exit 6** naming the flag. `use` and `which` scan the whole list with flags anywhere and the **last** version named winning, and `use --` names the version next and ends the scan. `ls`, `ls-remote`, `version` and `version-remote` scan the whole list and the **first** pattern named wins. `run` and `exec` stop at the first non-option, because everything after the version is the command's own argument list and a `--silent` there belongs to the command. `uninstall`, `reinstall-packages` and `copy-packages` scan the whole list and take exactly one version, a second being the usage refusal. Three smaller rules come with it, each nvm's own: a flag nvm says may be given once (`--save`, `--default`, `--reinstall-packages-from=`) is exit 6 when repeated rather than last-one-wins; `--reinstall-packages-from` is accepted only as `--flag=<version>`, the space spelling being exit 6, because a bare flag would swallow the version; and an unknown long option is refused (exit 55) by `exec`, `ls`, `ls-remote` and `version-remote`, while `run` hands it to node. **Why the differential suite did not catch this**: not one case asked for a flag after the version, so the shim's "stop at the first non-option" loop dropped every flag behind it and exited 0 having done nothing. `conformance/vibenvm/cases/17-flags-after-the-version.toml` now asks each wish in both positions, with the version file in the record, so the two positions are compared rather than assumed.

p.VIBENVM-BUILT-IN-ALIASES: **Decided 2026-11-11, after `nvm use default` was found exiting 3.** The `nvm alias` row of `#VIBENVM-MAPPING` says the built-in aliases map while named user aliases stay deferred — "`default` is the slot default, `node`/`stable` and `lts/*` are channels, `system` is #slot-off" — and that is a claim about the **version spellings every subcommand accepts**, not only about the `alias` verb it sits under. The shim honoured three of the four: `default` was handed to vibe as written, where it reads as a channel nothing declares, so `nvm use default` answered "`default` is not installed; run `nvm install default`" and exited 3 even with the slot default set. `default` is now one more spelling of the translation table: it resolves to `=<the slot's default version>`, read out of vibe's own `vibe app versions <slot> --installed --json` answer, which is free of a registry and of the network; with no default set it is the refusal that names how to set one. The spelling therefore works wherever a version does — `use`, `which`, `run`, `exec`, `version`, `install`, `uninstall` — because it is translated in one place and nothing downstream knows it was ever a word. An `lts/` **pattern** is likewise an LTS selection rather than a version pattern, as it is for nvm, so `nvm ls-remote lts/jod` and `nvm ls-remote --lts=jod` are one question and become one `--channel`. Nothing here resolves a version: the slot default is vibe's own fact and the shim reads it.

p.VIBENVM-GAPS: **Rewritten 2026-11-10 after the owner's decisions of that day — the count was three and is no longer three, and the honest arithmetic is below.** The fact this replaces said "the mapping yields exactly three new vibe features" and listed two of them plus "nothing else". Two things changed it, and neither is a failure of the mapping. **First, the owner rejected two of the fourteen proposed exclusions.** `nvm install --skip-default-packages` and `$NVM_DIR/default-packages` are not gaps vibe may decline; they are a general feature (`#SLOT-EXTRAS`). So the nvm surface now yields **three gaps**, not two: `--save` / `-w`, `--latest-npm` / `install-latest-npm`, and the default-packages pair. **Second, the owner required that nothing added for nvm know anything about npm or Node**, because the next pass replaces sdkman for Java and must land on the same machinery. Generalised under that rule, the three gaps become **four** general features, because two of them generalise into different shapes and one mechanism absorbs two gaps at once: (1) **`format = "keyed"` version files** — a file of `key = version` pairs in which each slot edits only its own line, which `.sdkmanrc`, `.tool-versions` and `mise.toml` all are (`#VERSION-FILE-KEYED`); (2) **`--write-version-file` for both formats**, which is `--save` / `-w` and which a version manager that reads a version file simply ought to have (`#VERSION-FILE-WRITE`); (3) **the ecosystem adapter** — a runtime package declaring how to install, list, remove and self-upgrade the packages of its *own* ecosystem, which absorbs `--latest-npm` (`self_upgrade`), `--reinstall-packages-from` (`list` then `install`, so the hand-written `npm-globals` migration becomes the general case) and the default-packages pair, in one declaration that names no ecosystem vibe knows (`#ECOSYSTEM-ADAPTER`, `#ECOSYSTEM-RECOMMENDS`, `#ECOSYSTEM-MIGRATION`); and (4) **the user's per-slot extras list** with its two flags and its command family (`#SLOT-EXTRAS`). **Two more general features are in phase P7 and are not demanded by nvm at all**, and saying so is the point of this fact: `[recommends]` on application packages with the general `--no-recommends` (PROP-077), and PROP-065's multi-step installation reaching ordinary packages (PROP-065 `#ordinary-reach`, with `B-188` as its first consumer). The owner decided both on 2026-11-10 as part of the same generalisation; they are campaign work, not proof work, and the differential suite neither needs nor exercises them. **One thing the proposal contained and the owner's refinement removed**: a general package-action verb (`vibe app action SLOT ID`) is **not** built, because every maintenance act the survey found is one of the adapter's four verbs — the reasoning, including the concrete reason building it on `[[application.migration]]` would have been wrong, is `#PACKAGE-ACTIONS`. **What survives of the original claim, and what does not.** The campaign's central prediction was that nvm's surface is absorbed by general machinery with no fourth gap discovered while writing the cases; the absorption held — nvm's own surface still yields three gaps and nothing else, and every other row of `#VIBENVM-MAPPING` is `maps` or an owner-approved `exclude` — but "exactly three new vibe features" is **false as written** and is corrected here rather than quietly reinterpreted: the generalisation requirement turned three gaps into four features, and the owner's own two additions brought phase P7's total to six. The named user aliases remain the one deferral `#VERSIONS-OPEN` records, and every remaining `exclude` row is nvm-internal state or a decision vibe takes globally (colour, progress, diagnostics, build mode). **Measured 2026-11-11, when the shim was built and the suite ran against it: the count is still four plus two, and no new feature was needed.** Every row of `#VIBENVM-MAPPING` marked `maps` was expressible with the surface sections 2–4 already have, every row marked `needs` was answered by one of the four general features, and the twelve approved `exclude` rows are the whole of what vibenvm refuses — so the campaign's central prediction ("no seventh feature is discovered while writing the cases") held. What the construction did surface is **four honest shortfalls of features that exist**, none of them a new feature and none of them patched inside the shim: `vibe install -g` of an application with no version named does not consult the declared version file though this document's own precedence puts it there; `vibe app versions` has no version-pattern filter, so nvm's `ls <pattern>` answers with the one version a requirement resolves to rather than every match; `--write-version-file` exists only on commands that change state, so nvm's `use --save` — which changes the shell and the file and *not* the global default — moves the slot default with it; and a version file's bare `22.9.0` is read as a caret requirement, so the file `--write-version-file` has just written stops pinning the version it recorded as soon as a newer minor is installed. All four are `#P7F-AS-BUILT` (4) and the campaign's backlog, and the honest reading of them is that the nvm surface is covered while three of its conveniences cost the shim an extra composition and one is a semantic wart the suite does not catch.

p.VIBENVM-SUITE: **Decided 2026-11-10 — the differential suite.** It lives at `conformance/vibenvm/` in this repository, driven by `cargo xtask vibenvm-conform` and by `conformance/vibenvm/run.sh` directly; **its verdict is its exit code** and no part of it reads or writes a model's opinion. **Isolation.** One temporary root per case, two sandboxes inside it: `A` with `HOME=<root>/a` and `NVM_DIR=<root>/a/.nvm` holding the pinned nvm-sh checkout, `B` with `HOME=<root>/b`, `VIBE_SETTINGS=<root>/b/.vibe` and the `vibenvm` package installed, both started from a `PATH` reduced to a fixed minimal list, both with every `NVM_*` and `VIBE_*` variable of the invoking environment removed, as `crates/vibe-test-support`'s `UserScratch` already does for the CLI tests. **The local Node release mirror.** `conformance/vibenvm/fetch-mirror.sh` populates a git-ignored `mirror/` once with `dist/index.json` and, for a pinned small set of versions (two in one major, one older major, one LTS line), `dist/v<V>/SHASUMS256.txt` and the Linux x64 archive; every file's SHA-256 is pinned in a committed `mirror.lock` and the suite refuses to run on a mismatch. The suite then serves `mirror/` over loopback HTTP and **makes no internet access at all**: `A` is pointed at it with `NVM_NODEJS_ORG_MIRROR`, and `B` with a remap row for `nodejs.org` in its own settings (PROP-066 `#locator`), which is the mechanism a closed network uses anyway — so the suite exercises the real path rather than a test-only flag. A non-loopback connection attempt fails the run. **A case** is a TOML file under `cases/`: `commands = [ … ]`, each a shell line in which the token `nvm` is the tool under test, run in both sandboxes in order. **After every step**, each sandbox writes one observation record: `exit`; `node_v` and `npm_v` (the output of `node -v` / `npm -v`, or `absent`); `which_node` (`command -v node`, normalised); `owned_path` (the ordered PATH entries under the tool's own root, normalised); `installed` (the sorted installed version list); `default` (the resolved default); `aliases` (sorted `name=target` pairs, from `$NVM_DIR/alias/**` for `A` and from the slot state plus channels for `B`); and `globals` (for each installed version, `npm ls -g --depth 0 --parseable` reduced to sorted `name@version` pairs). That is the owner's list, mechanised. **Normalisations** are declared, mechanical and in one file `normalise.rules`: absolute sandbox paths to `<HOME>`, the tool root to `<TOOLROOT>`, ANSI SGR sequences stripped, `\d+(\.\d+)?(ms|s)` to `<T>`, download-progress and npm-notice lines dropped by a listed regex, and version lists sorted. **The comparison is of observation records, field by field; stdout and stderr text are not compared at all** unless a case sets `compare_stdout = true`, and then only after the same normalisations — which is what keeps an LLM out of the verdict. **The coverage gate.** `extract-inventory.sh` re-extracts the subcommand and flag inventory from the pinned `nvm.sh` (the dispatch `case` patterns and the flag patterns inside each branch) into `inventory.json`; `coverage.py` requires every `(subcommand, flag)` pair in it to be covered by at least one **passing** case or to appear in `exclusions.toml` as an owner-approved entry. **Reusing nvm's own tests**: the pinned `test/fast/` suite is the near-offline part (it stubs `nvm_download` and friends and compares against recorded mocks in `test/fast/Unit tests/mocks/`), and the suite runs the subset of it that exercises only the public `nvm` function, against `vibenvm`, under `urchin`; the few `fast` tests that reach the network and all of `slow/`, `installation_*/`, `sourcing/`, `install_script/` and `xenial/` are out of scope and listed as such, with the subset recorded in a committed `nvm-tests.allow`. **Exit codes**: `0` every case passed and coverage is complete; `1` a differential mismatch, with the case, the step, the field and both values; `2` coverage incomplete, naming each uncovered pair; `3` a harness error (mirror digest mismatch, a non-loopback connection attempt, a missing pinned tag). The suite is Linux-only and says so; it is not a cross-platform claim. **The harness half is implemented 2026-11-10 (campaign phase P7f), and what keeps this fact `impl/work` is named at the end.** It is `conformance/vibenvm/` driven by `cargo xtask vibenvm-conform [--cases GLOB] [--update-inventory]` and by `run.sh` directly, and its exit code is the verdict with nothing else in the loop. **Isolation, as built.** `run.sh` re-executes itself inside `bwrap --dev-bind / / --proc /proc --unshare-net --unshare-pid`, where only loopback exists, and every case runs under `env -i` with `PATH=/usr/bin:/bin`, its own `HOME`, `TMPDIR` and `LC_ALL=C` — so no `NVM_*` or `VIBE_*` of the invoking environment survives — and under `strace -f -e trace=connect`, where any `connect(2)` that is not a unix socket, netlink, `127.0.0.0/8` or `::1` fails the run with exit 3 although it could not have succeeded. Two guards the design did not foresee were needed to keep that true: npm's registry is pointed at an empty loopback directory (`npm_config_registry`), and so is nvm's io.js mirror (`NVM_IOJS_ORG_MIRROR`), because nvm's default category set includes `iojs` and `ls-remote` would otherwise ask nodejs.org's io.js sibling. Both then answer a deterministic 404 instead of reaching out. **A case's steps run in one shell**, not one per step, because the state a version manager exists to change — `PATH` above all — has to carry from step to step the way it does for a user. **The mirror.** `fetch-mirror.sh` is the only networked step, reaches `nodejs.org` and `github.com` only, verifies the pinned tag object itself, and pins 17 files by SHA-256 in `mirror.lock`: the four node versions' `SHASUMS256.txt` and Linux x64 archives in both `tar.xz` and `tar.gz` (nvm chooses by what the host's `tar` and `xz` support), `nvm.sh`, `nvm-exec`, `bash_completion`, and the two indexes. The indexes are **filtered to the pinned version set** — a mirror describes what the mirror has, and an unfiltered `index.json` changes with every Node release and so could never be pinned by digest. The set is `v23.1.0`, `v22.11.0` (Jod), `v22.9.0` and `v20.18.0` (Iron), which is the two-in-one-major plus older-major plus LTS-line shape this fact asks for, and it also makes `--lts`, `--lts=<name>` and the `node` channel resolve to things the mirror holds. `index.tab` is mirrored as well as `index.json`, because nvm reads the former and vibe the latter. **The inventory.** The re-extraction yields **76 pairs over 23 subcommands** from v0.41.0; 24 of them are excluded by the owner's approved items and **52 are required and covered** by nine cases. Three spelling rules the extraction had to settle: a flag carries no `=` and no value (`--lts` and `--lts=*` are one flag); a branch's flags are recorded against the branch's first (canonical) subcommand spelling, because the alias enters the same branch and the flags are parsed once; and an alias spelling (`i`, `list`, `list-remote`, `copy-packages`, `-v`, `help`, `--help`) therefore gets a bare pair of its own, so the gate still asks for a case per alias. Coverage is **derived from the command lines the cases actually ran**, canonicalised the same way, and only from cases that passed — a case covers what it runs, never what it claims. **The observation record** is a sorted `field<TAB>value` file, so the comparison is a field-by-field read rather than a JSON walk, and fields whose name starts with `_` (the step number and the command line) are the reader's and are never compared. Two deviations, both earned: the record gained a **`file:<path>` field family** driven by a case's `observe_files`, without which `install --save` could only be observed as "exited 0" and the version file it wrote would not be compared at all; and the tool's own root comes from the harness, not from `$NVM_DIR` in the shell, because `nvm unload` unsets its own variables and an observation that went blind at exactly the step that matters would compare nothing. **One normalisation earns its own sentence**: a version's directory under the tool root collapses to `<TOOLROOT>@v<version>`, so `which_node` and `owned_path` compare as what they are — the directory of a specific version — without either tool's directory layout winning. **The meta-tests all behave**: a perturbed field is exit 1 naming the field and both values, an uncovered pair is exit 2 naming the pair, an unapproved exclusion row and a row beyond the owner's closed set are each exit 2, a tampered `mirror.lock` is exit 3, and a real non-loopback `connect(2)` attempt is seen by the guard. **What keeps this fact `impl/work`.** Sandbox B is wired in full — its own `HOME` and `VIBE_SETTINGS`, the `[[remap]]` row for `nodejs.org`, and `vibe install -g org.vibevm.node/vibenvm` from a local registry — but the shim package does not exist yet, so a default run reports a **harness error (exit 3) naming the missing package** rather than a pass or a mismatch, and the B-side observation adapter and the layout collapse have never been exercised against vibe's own output. `urchin` is not installed on the machine this was built on, so the `test/fast` reuse is recorded in `nvm-tests.allow` and run by nothing. And it is Linux-only, as this fact already says.

p.VIBENVM-EXCLUSIONS: **Decided 2026-11-10 — the exclusion list format.** `conformance/vibenvm/exclusions.toml`, `schema = 1`, one `[[exclusion]]` row per entry with `subcommand` (as the dispatch spells it), `flag` (as `nvm.sh` spells it; an empty string excludes the whole subcommand), `reason` (one sentence), `approved_by` and `approved` (an RFC 3339 date). **A row without `approved_by = "owner"` and a date does not count as approved and the coverage gate fails on it**, so a worker cannot widen the exclusion list and an unreviewed exclusion cannot pass as reviewed. The rows the design proposes are exactly the `exclude` verdicts of `#VIBENVM-MAPPING`, each with that row's reason; the owner approves or rejects them one by one, and a rejection turns that row into a `needs` — a named new vibe feature — which is the only other way out. The file is read by `coverage.py` and by nothing else, and it is committed, so the set of accepted gaps is visible in the git log of one file, the way `formats/EPOCHS.toml` makes a stability claim visible. **Implemented 2026-11-10 (campaign phase P7f's harness half), with one addition and one residue.** `conformance/vibenvm/exclusions.toml` carries the owner's twelve approved items as **fourteen `[[exclusion]]` rows**, which is this fact's own row rule (1) applied rather than bent: `install -s` and `install -b` are two rows sharing one reason, and the internal-state item is recorded under both the `(environment)` and the `(internal)` spelling `#VIBENVM-EXCLUSIONS-APPROVED` prescribes. **The addition** is a sixth key, `item`, naming which approved item a row belongs to, so the twelve stay countable in a file of fourteen rows; `coverage.py` checks the item count as well as the rows. **The closure is mechanical, not a matter of review**: `coverage.py` holds the set of approved `(subcommand, flag)` rows and fails (exit 2) on any row that is not one of them, on any row missing `approved_by = "owner"` or an RFC 3339 date, on a duplicate, and on a row the extraction yields no pair for — so a worker can neither widen the list nor quietly reword it, and a thirteenth accepted gap is a gate failure in the one file whose git log shows the decision. The two rows the owner rejected are absent, and `cases/16-default-packages.toml` covers them instead. **What keeps this fact `impl/work`:** the gate that reads the file has so far only ever run with sandbox A on both sides, so no row has yet had the chance to hide a real divergence, and the `item` key is an addition this fact does not itself describe.

p.VIBENVM-PORTABILITY: **Decided 2026-11-12 — the shim is sourced on two userlands, and the suite can only see one of them.** Release testing on a real Mac found `nvm install 26` answering `Version '26' not found` while `vibe install -g org.vibevm.node/node@26` worked in the same shell. The cause was one character: the reader of vibe's planned version used `\?`, which is a GNU extension in a **basic** regular expression — GNU sed matches it, BSD sed, which macOS ships, never does — so the reader produced nothing and every command that resolves a version remotely failed. Two neighbouring readers in the same file already used the portable form, so this was a slip rather than a design error, which is exactly the kind a review does not catch. **The differential suite structurally cannot catch this class**: it is Linux-only by construction, needing `bwrap --unshare-net` for the network isolation and `strace` for the proof that nothing reached past loopback, so a GNU-only construct passes all of its cases and tells us nothing about the other half of the platforms the package declares. The answer is therefore not another case but a **gate on the class**: `portability.sh` in the package refuses the constructs a BSD userland has not — `\?`, `\+`, `\|` in a BRE, `sed -i`, `grep -P`, `sort -V`, `readlink -f`, `date -d`, `head -n -N`, `\s` / `\w`, the gawk-only functions, `echo -e`, `seq`, `mktemp -p` — in either quote style, and `run.sh` runs it as a sandbox-B prerequisite so the suite **refuses to return a verdict** for a shim that fails it rather than returning one that means nothing about macOS. It is proven to fail on planted constructs and to pass on the shim, which is the property that matters for a gate. What stays unproven and is not claimed: the suite's shim side has never run under a BSD userland, because this machine has none; the real-Mac evidence is a hand run, and the gate is a static check, and neither is the suite.

p.VIBENVM-NO-EXCLUSIONS: **Decided 2026-11-11 by the owner, and it supersedes `#VIBENVM-EXCLUSIONS-APPROVED`.** The owner reopened the twelve approved gaps and closed them the other way: «Можно ли сделать так, чтобы все остальные части vibenvm были реализованы тоже, но уже на уровне самого пакета … vibenvm это не честный шим поверх нвм, он не реализует всей функциональности» — every excluded nvm surface is to be **implemented inside the package** (and inside the Node package), not left as an accepted gap and not paid for by widening vibe's core except where a small general core feature is genuinely needed. Two such features were needed and are built: `#TEMPLATE-NO-DIGEST` and `#TEMPLATE-IN-A-REPO`. The package is renamed and re-shaped by two further decisions of the same day: «неплохо бы сделать так, чтобы наш vibenvm имел ту же версию, что и nvm которого он изображает», answered by «Делаем шаблонным, снимаем версии, сам пакет называем org.vibevm.nvm/nvm» — the shim becomes a **template package** whose produced versions **are nvm's own**, so `nvm --version` prints the nvm release it implements and a shim fix ships as a new template **revision** rather than as a change to a published version's content; and «сборку из исходников тоже делаем» — the Node template gains a `source` installer option, so `nvm install -s` maps onto a real build rather than onto a refusal. The accepted-gap set is therefore **empty**, `conformance/vibenvm/exclusions.toml` is deleted, and `coverage.py`'s closed set is `frozenset()`: the machinery stays precisely so that a row added back is not in the closed set and fails the gate — reintroducing an exclusion is a change to the gate's own source, under the owner's eye, never a row dropped into a data file beside it. `#VIBENVM-EXCLUSIONS-APPROVED` remains in this document as the record of what was decided on 2026-11-10 and why it was reversed, not as a live rule.

p.VIBENVM-EXCLUSIONS-APPROVED: **Owner decision 2026-11-10 — twelve exclusions approved, two rejected, and the exact rows the suite commits.** The design proposed fourteen; the owner approved twelve and rejected two. Every row below is written into `conformance/vibenvm/exclusions.toml` with `approved_by = "owner"` and `approved = "2026-11-10"`, the reason it carries here, and nothing else; `#VIBENVM-EXCLUSIONS` makes any further row a gate failure, so this list is closed until the owner reopens it. **Approved, in the owner's own five groups.** *Named user aliases (five)*: `nvm alias [<pattern>] / <name> <version>`; `nvm unalias <name>`; `nvm install --alias=<name>`; `nvm ls --no-alias`; and nvm's own alias store `$NVM_DIR/alias/*`. The reason is one the owner had already given and a survey confirmed: named user aliases are built in to only 5 of the 17 switchers surveyed (nvm, fnm, rvm, mise, jabba), 6 reach them only by a plugin or a workaround (pyenv, rbenv, asdf, rustup, sdkman, jenv) and 6 have none at all (volta, n, goenv, gvm, Coursier, uv) — the newest tools among them — so they are not a must-have, and the one alias everyone really uses, `default`, is the slot default vibe already has, while `lts` / `latest` / `stable` are channels (`#CHANNEL-SYNTAX`). They stay deferred by `#VERSIONS-OPEN`; if they are ever built it is as one general feature for every application, which closes these five rows on its own. *Source build (two)*: `nvm install -s` / `-b` and `nvm install -j <N>`. vibe selects an installer option, never a build mode, and the Node template publishes only upstream's prebuilt archives, so `-b` is always true and `-s` / `-j` have nothing to apply to; the feature that would close them is filed as `B-253` (a source-build installer option with declared parallelism), recorded and deliberately not done. *Version categories and nvm-internal state (two)*: `nvm install --only=<categories>`, and `$NVM_ONLY` with `.lts-status`, nvm's per-version install locks, `$NVM_AUTH_HEADER` and its third-party installer hook. This is the owner's answer to `#OWNER-QUESTIONS` Q2: `lts` is a channel, `alpha` is `prerelease = "include"` on the template, `iojs` is a dead product and `non-lts` serves no scenario, so a general "version class" concept in vibe would be weight carried for one dead product; the state items are nvm's own internals, against which vibe has its own locks and its own authorisation (PROP-066). *Prefix hygiene, colours and diagnostics (three)*: `nvm use --delete-prefix`, because `$PREFIX` / `$NPM_CONFIG_PREFIX` is nvm's conflict with itself and vibe owns its own install root and PATH; `nvm set-colors`, because the colour decision is PROP-060 `#DISPLAY`'s for every command and a per-tool palette would break that one decision; and `nvm debug`, because vibe's diagnostic is `vibe self doctor` and nvm's dump enumerates nvm's internals, against which there is nothing to compare. **Rejected (two), and what they became.** `nvm install --skip-default-packages` and `$NVM_DIR/default-packages` are **not** exclusions: the owner ruled them a general feature, `#SLOT-EXTRAS`, so both rows are now `maps` in `#VIBENVM-MAPPING` and the suite must cover them with real differential cases. **Three rules the row format needs, stated here rather than discovered by whoever writes the file.** (1) The gate's unit is an extracted `(subcommand, flag)` pair, so an approved item that names two flags is two rows sharing one reason — `install -s` and `install -b` are two. (2) `subcommand = "*"` is admitted and means every verb on which the extraction finds that flag, which is what `--only=` needs, because the pinned v0.41.0 carries it on nearly every verb and twenty rows with one reason would hide rather than show the decision. (3) An item the extraction does not yield as a pair at all — an environment variable or an internal file — is recorded with `subcommand = "(environment)"` or `"(internal)"` and is **reported as recorded, not required**: the file then documents the whole accepted-gap set, while the gate stays driven by what the pinned tree actually yields, so no row can silently satisfy a pair the extraction never found.

p.VERSIONS-OPEN: Deferred by the owner and still deferred: **named user aliases** (`nvm alias foo 22`). The built-in aliases map onto existing concepts (`#VIBENVM-MAPPING`), **Confirmed and evidenced 2026-11-10**: a survey of 17 switchers found named user aliases built in to only 5 of them (nvm, fnm, rvm, mise, jabba), reachable by a plugin or a workaround in 6 (pyenv, rbenv, asdf, rustup, sdkman, jenv) and absent from 6 (volta, n, goenv, gvm, Coursier, uv) — including the newest, which is the shape of a feature that is not a must-have. The deferral costs the shim **five** owner-approved `exclude` rows (`#VIBENVM-EXCLUSIONS-APPROVED`) and nothing else, because the built-in aliases map onto existing concepts; if named aliases are ever built it is as one general feature for every application, in the form mise uses — an alias as a named version request in the same namespace as channels — and it closes those five rows on its own. Everything else VERSIONS-OPEN listed on 2026-11-09 — the manifest spelling and the source-kind set, the channel syntax in requirements and lock records, the snapshot layout and its staleness rules, whether rendering happens at resolution or at publication, the hook implementation per shell and its cost budget, and the migration step inputs and failure semantics — is decided above.

p.OWNER-QUESTIONS: **Open to the owner, each with the default the design takes unless the owner says otherwise. Q1 and Q2 are answered; Q3, Q4 and Q5 stand on their defaults.** (Q1) **ANSWERED 2026-11-10.** The exclusion list needed the owner's approval row by row, because `#VIBENVM-EXCLUSIONS` makes an unapproved row a gate failure by construction. The owner reviewed all fourteen: **twelve are approved** with the reasons given and **two are rejected** — `--skip-default-packages` and `$NVM_DIR/default-packages`, which became the general ecosystem-adapter and slot-extras feature instead. The approved set, its exact rows and the three row-format rules the file needs are `#VIBENVM-EXCLUSIONS-APPROVED`; nothing may be added to it without the owner. (Q2) **ANSWERED 2026-11-10 — excluded, as the design proposed.** `--only=<categories>` was the largest single exclusion: nvm's four-way taxonomy (`alpha`, `lts`, `non-lts`, `iojs`) is nvm-internal, and the design maps `lts` to a channel, `alpha` to the template's `prerelease = "include"` and drops `iojs` and `non-lts`. The owner approved the exclusion, so the alternative — a general "version class" concept in vibe — is **not** built, and the risk P7 carried that rejecting it would grow the campaign by a phase is withdrawn. (Q3) The version-list TTL default of 15 minutes (`#TEMPLATE-CACHE`) is a guess at the right trade between a stale list and a network call on every resolution; the default stands and is one line in `~/.vibe/config.toml`. (Q4) `#TEMPLATE-DISCOVERY` makes a template undiscoverable in a per-package git registry with no index, refusing with `template_index_required`; the default is to accept that limitation, since the real registry has an index and a closed network uses a layout registry, and the alternative costs one fetch per tag. (Q5) `#TEMPLATE-LOCK-RECORD` gives the changed-digest alarm **no** `--trust-template` escape hatch; the default is no hatch, on the grounds that both legitimate causes have an honest answer and PROP-002's mirror hatch is about availability rather than content.

p.P2-AS-BUILT: **Implemented 2026-11-10 (campaign phase P2) — what the code decided that the design left open or stated differently.** Eight amendments, each a consequence of the actual tree rather than a change of intent. **(1) Where lowering happens.** `#CHANNEL-SYNTAX` names the entry paths that call `lower_channel`. As built the one named function is called at the **registry resolution seam** every one of those paths passes through (`LocalRegistry::resolve`, which the `--registry DIR` path, a configured `file://` `localdir` source and a `monorepo` working copy all reach — spike S2's three paths). That is strictly stronger than a list of call sites, because no entry path can forget it, and it leaves the solver exactly as untouched: an unlowered channel still matches nothing, `SemverVersionSet::from_spec` is still the empty set, and every other `VersionSpec` read site either lowers first or refuses rather than picks, so a path that bypasses the seam fails closed rather than installing something plausible. The survey named eight such sites; `VersionSpec` is in fact read across eighteen files, and because the enum is matched **exhaustively** in every one of them the compiler enumerated the list — which is what made the fail-closed design cost nothing to adopt. The reserved `latest` and `stable` are answered by `lower_channel` itself from the domain, so every package has them declared or not. **(2) How the lock learns what the resolver did.** `ResolvedPackage` is the type the four call sites of `#TEMPLATE-DOMAIN-SEAM` hand back untouched, and widening it would have touched every construction site in the tree for a fact two of them have. Instead the layer **notes** what it did for one `(package, version)` — the full render's lock record and the channel the requirement lowered through — and the fetch reads that note onto `CachedPackage`, whence the ordinary lock writer carries it. Both halves are `None` for an ordinary published package under an ordinary requirement, which is what keeps a lock with no template byte-identical. **(3) One more file in the cache, and why it is not a cached render.** `#TEMPLATE-CACHE`'s directory gains `template.toml`, the template **document** verbatim. It is a declaration, not an output, so `#TEMPLATE-RENDER-LOCATION`'s ban stands; it exists because `#ACTIVATION-HOOK` forbids the hook's one call a registry read, and lowering a channel needs the `[[template.channel]]` rules. With the declaration cached beside the version list, a channel is lowered from two small file reads and nothing else — which is how a `.nvmrc` holding `lts/jod` now resolves (AV-FMT-024, completing P5a's `unresolved_channel`). Unlike a digest document it is **not** write-once: a template can be fixed without touching a produced version, and the cache must then hold the fix. **(4) A cache is derived state, and is treated as such.** A corrupt `versions.json` reads as **absent** rather than fatal, and a fetch that fails over a merely-aged copy logs once and uses it: the version list is advisory and the digests are what bind, so refusing would strand a user behind a file they never wrote. A rendered directory is rebuilt rather than reused, because a half-written one from an interrupted run must not be installed from. **(5) The remap-source epoch floor had to be named.** The lockfile's 9 → 10 step broke `validate_remap_sources`, which read its floor off `CURRENT_SCHEMA_VERSION`; the floor is now its own `REMAP_SOURCE_SCHEMA_VERSION = 9`. Recorded because the next epoch step will meet the same hazard, and because it is the one place the 7 → 8 → 9 precedent was *not* already followed. **(6) `[package] channels` refuses on a template.** `#CHANNEL-SYNTAX` gives a concrete package publisher-assigned labels and a template derived channels; as built the two may not appear on one manifest, because two mechanisms deciding one package's channels is a question with no right answer. The refusal names `[package].channels` and points at `[[template.channel]]`. **(7) The version-list fetch is not the alarm's business.** `#TEMPLATE-LOCK-RECORD`'s alarm is raised by `verify_recorded`, which recomputes the **full** render and compares `rendered_sha256`; the recomputation reads the digest document, and the cached one is immutable, so re-verifying a version already installed costs nothing and a changed upstream document is the alarm rather than a race. A template revision alone, with the same produced version and the same digests, verifies — the hash binds, not the revision, which is TEMPLATE-FLAG's whole purpose. **(8) Which registries see a template, as built.** Discovery is implemented for every **directory-shaped** registry — `--registry DIR`, a `localdir` source, a `monorepo` working copy, a mirrored layout registry — by reading the manifests on disk, which is the answer `#TEMPLATE-DISCOVERY` prescribes for them and which `vibe_index::layout::project` derives its index from, so the indexed and the layout path agree by construction. The index member that carries the fact for a **per-package git** registry is delivered (AV-FMT-003, `version_entry.template`), and the refusal that path needs is written (`template_index_required`), but rendering a template fetched from a per-package git registry is **not** wired: it is the one part of this fact P2 leaves to the phase that first needs it, named here rather than discovered later. The real registry has an index and a closed network uses a layout registry, which is why the owner's own Q4 accepted the narrower surface.
