p.P5A-AS-BUILT: **Implemented 2026-11-10 (campaign phase P5a) — what the code decided that the design left open or stated differently.** Nine amendments, each a consequence of the actual tree rather than a change of intent. **(1) Where the declared version files live.** `#ACTIVATION-HOOK` requires the hook's one call to read "the home's index and the version files only", so the declared `[[application.version_file]]` rows must be retained by the home. They are kept **beside** the index, in `<settings>/applications/version-files.json` with protocol `vibe-app-version-files/1`, not inside it: putting them in the index record would move the inventory to `vibe-user-applications/7` and so require the `vibe-app-proxy` admission of PROP-059 `#proxy-index-upgrade`, which `#FORMAT-CHANGES` assigns wholly to `AV-FMT-017` in phase P2. `Index::load` reads the sidecar into the records and every publication rewrites it from them, so an uninstalled key simply stops being declared and the two documents cannot diverge. A missing or corrupt sidecar is an empty declared set, which degrades to "this slot has no version file". **(2) The resolution cache is its own registered format**, `<home>/cache/version-files.json`, `vibe-app-version-file-cache/1`: one entry per directory with every path consulted, its modification time and size (or its recorded absence) and the selection that resulted. **(3) Channels in P5a.** `#CHANNEL-SYNTAX` reserves `latest` and `stable` for every package; over an installed set they need neither a network nor a template, so both are lowered here. Every other channel — `lts`, `lts/jod` — parses, is carried as a channel, and resolves to the reported state `unresolved_channel` until the channel resolver of phase P2 exists. That is why `#VERSION-FILE-FORMATS` and `#VERSION-EXEC-SPELLING` are `impl/work` and not `impl/done`. **(4) A leading `v` is tolerated** before a version requirement in a version file (`v22.23.4`), because that is the spelling `.nvmrc` files and upstream tags actually carry; the authored spelling is kept for every report. **(5) "Nothing narrows it".** A requirement that several installed versions satisfy resolves to the **newest** of them, which is what a version manager means by `use 22`; `selection_required` is raised only when several distinct installations share that newest version, which is the case nothing in the request can narrow. **(6) `vibe app env --project` retracts as well as applies.** It makes `PATH` match the directory, so a selection the inherited `VIBE_APP_USE` carries and this resolution does not re-apply is taken out. Without that the prompt hook could never undo anything on leaving a project, and `#ACTIVATION-HOOK`'s "a previously applied selection must be undone" would have no mechanism. **(7) The project root is the nearest ancestor** holding a `vibe.toml`, found from anywhere inside the project — `commands::app::home::project_at`, which answers for the project *home* scope of PROP-059 `#project-scope`, requires the directory itself to hold one, and a version-file search that stopped only at its own directory would never stop at all. **(8) `vibe app exec` replaces this process** on a POSIX host (`exec`), which is the strongest form of `#VERSION-EXEC-SPELLING`'s "the child inherits the standard streams, its exit status passes through unchanged and POSIX signals are forwarded": there is no parent left to lose a signal. Windows spawns and waits, as it must. **(9) Notices go to stderr.** `vibe app env` prints its lines on stdout and nothing else, so everything the resolution reported — a version that is not installed with its exact install command, an unusable version-file line, a `.tool-versions` line's unused versions — is written to stderr, where a prompt hook's `eval` cannot choke on it. Not implemented by P5a, and still `spec/plan`: `#VERSIONS-LIST-OUTPUT` (phase P5b) and `--write-version-file` (`#VIBENVM-GAPS`, phase P7).

p.P5B-AS-BUILT: **Implemented 2026-11-10 (campaign phase P5b) — what the code decided that `#VERSIONS-LIST-OUTPUT` left open.** Five amendments. **(1) The listing is a join across one seam, and the seam is a trait.** `vibe app versions` is the only surface that needs a package’s whole domain *and* this home’s inventory, and the two live in different crates. As built, `vibe-app` owns the join (`versions_listing`) and takes the domain through a `Domains` trait it never implements, so the library reaches no registry, no index server and no socket, and a test states a domain outright. The CLI implements the trait over the same source chain an install resolves through. That is why `--installed` can be free of the network by construction rather than by care: it hands the join a cache-only implementor. **(2) The JSON tokens are not the human spellings.** `#VERSIONS-LIST-OUTPUT` writes the origin `published (overrides template)` and the state `installed (default)`. A closed JTD vocabulary cannot carry a space or a parenthesis, so the wire tokens are `overrides` and `installed_default` and the parenthesised forms are their rendering (`AV-FMT-014`). The human line is unchanged from the fact; only the machine answer differs, and it differs the way every other closed vocabulary in the tree does. **(3) A bare argument resolves in three steps, and refuses rather than guesses.** A `<group>/<name>` is itself; a bare word is a slot of this home when one is recorded, and a slot with providers from several packages lists each under its own heading; otherwise the word is matched against the installed packages’ names, and a word several of them carry is `ambiguous_target` naming the `<group>/<name>` spellings while a word nothing carries is `unknown_target` naming the slots that do exist. The fact asked for «the ordinary refusal that names the spellings, never a guess»; as built that is two codes rather than one, because the two situations have different fixes. A version pinned onto the coordinate (`org.vibevm.node/node@22`) is accepted and ignored: the listing is about a package, never about one version of it. **(4) An installation the domain no longer carries is still a row.** The rows are the **union** of the domain and this home’s installations, not the domain filtered. A version whose registry row was yanked, whose registry is gone, or which came from a registry this invocation cannot reach is still installed, and a listing that hid it would be lying about the home; such a row is `published` with its local state. **(5) `--channel` needs the channel table and therefore refuses an unknown name.** `#VERSIONS-LIST-OUTPUT` does not say what `--channel nonsense` does. As built it is `unknown_channel` naming the channels the package declares, the same posture `#CHANNEL-SYNTAX` takes for `@lts/argon`. Under `--installed` the table comes from the template cache alone, so a channel still narrows the installed set without a request. Two consequences of the tree, recorded rather than discovered later: the enumeration a listing needs is a new read-only seam on the app resolver (`versions_from_global_with_operation`, `directory_roots_from_global_with_operation`) because the existing one only ever resolved **one** version, the `snapshot_synced` member of `#MIRROR-SNAPSHOT-LAYOUT` is declared in the wire but left unfilled until P4 writes a snapshot for it to read; and the four refusals are their own `VersionsError` family rather than four more arms of `AppError`, because adding them in place carried that file past the 600-line conform limit — the sibling `error_paths` and `error_lifecycle` families exist for the same reason, `AppError` delegates transparently so no caller’s `match` changes, and `vibe app errors` lists the new table beside every other.

p.P3-AS-BUILT: **Implemented 2026-11-10 (campaign phase P3) — what the real Node package decided that the design left open or stated differently.** Four amendments; none changes an intent, each is what upstream's actual documents say. **(1) A third `template_optional` row, and the measurement behind it.** `#TEMPLATE-OPTION-GATING` names musl and Windows-ARM as the rows whose archives upstream does not always build; the frozen index says `macos-arm64` as well. Measured over the 406 produced versions of the declared window (`min = "12.0.0"` up to 26.13.0): `linux-x64-musl` is absent from 389 of them, `osx-arm64-tar` from 132 (Apple-silicon archives start at 16.0.0), `win-arm64-zip` from 234 (19.9.0), and all seven targets are present together only from 26.8.0 up. Without the third row every release below 16.0.0 — a third of the declared window — refuses to render instead of installing the targets it really has, and the two versions the golden comparison covers cannot see it. It was found while preparing exactly the case `PLAN.md` prescribed for this risk — rendering the oldest version in the `min` window — and that case is now a test in both suites. The rule the package now follows is in its own boot document — a required row upstream stops building must *become* optional, never disappear. **(2) Frozen upstream documents close the provenance chain the golden proof needed.** P1 derived the two digest documents by hand from the committed manifests, which made the golden comparison a statement about two renderers agreeing on seven digests somebody typed. P3 froze upstream's own `SHASUMS256.txt` for both versions, and each one hashes to exactly the value the committed manifest's provenance header records as the generator's input (`aec92ae9…`, `c90c3f14…`), so the claim is now the stronger one: the template and the retired generator render the same manifest **from the same bytes**, and `node_golden.rs` asserts that equality rather than assuming it. The version list is frozen the same way: upstream writes one record per line, newest first, so the committed subset is a **leading slice** of it (down to and including `v12.0.0`, the declared `min`, plus the next three records, which `min` must drop) with every kept record byte-verbatim — which makes the subset the template's *whole* version domain, so `lts`, `lts/jod` and `stable` answer with upstream's real answers rather than a doctored document's. The live hand install confirmed the freeze from the other side: the `index.json` the real run fetched hashes to the fixture's own SHA-256. **(3) A requirement is not a pin, and for a template that now decides which document is fetched.** `@12.0.0` is `^12.0.0` and resolves to 12.22.12, as it always has; what is new is that a template's domain is hundreds of versions rather than the handful a published package carries, so an inexact spelling silently moves the resolution to a different release *and* a different digest document. The oldest-version test therefore pins with `@=12.0.0`, and a user who means one release must spell it that way. **(4) The plan already costs the digest document, and the package is not republished yet.** `#TEMPLATE-TWO-STAGE` gives resolution one request and an install two; on the `install -g` path `--plan-only` nevertheless performs the **full** render, because `vibe_app::resolve::from_global_with_operation` resolves through `resolve_and_fetch` — the skeleton stage serves the depsolver's `fetch_manifest`, not the global plan. The suite relies on that: every case in `cli_template_node.rs` is a `--plan-only` run and still proves what was rendered. And the package stays unpublished for one reason, which is not a defect of P3: rendering a template found in a **per-package git registry** is the part of `#TEMPLATE-DISCOVERY` P2 left to the phase that first needs it, and P3 does not need it — it is proved over directory-shaped registries and by the hand install. The template revision is deliberately numbered `1.0.0`, below every produced version, so that even a template-unaware client walking the tags prefers a real Node.js version over the template itself.

p.P4-AS-BUILT: **Implemented 2026-11-10 (campaign phase P4) — what the code decided that section 3 left open or stated differently.** The phase is three atomic commits, all landed: **(a)** the declarative selection, **(b)** the `_index/templates/` snapshot writer, and **(c)** payload projection with its budget, `--dry-run` counts, the `--prune` surface and the report’s two arrays. Amendments 1–10 below are (a)'s and the cross-cutting ones, 11–16 are (b)'s, and 17–27 are (c)'s. **(1) Only a *declared* selection is recorded.** `#MIRROR-CONFIG-SCHEMA` writes "the effective selection — merged from the file and the flags" into `_index/mirrors/<source>.toml`. As built a `--config` run records its selection and a `--package` / `--group` run records nothing. The flag predates this feature and has a second job — making a source that can be listed neither by its index nor by its host’s organisation API mirrorable one package at a time — so recording it would turn that workaround into a permanent narrowing of every later bare run of that source, and would let one per-run override destroy the operator’s declaration. The trap was not hypothetical: implemented literally it turned an existing test red, because a leg that deliberately passed no `--package`, to prove the organisation listing opens once a token is configured, repeated a narrowing an earlier leg had recorded and listed by tags instead. It is also what keeps the record byte-identical for every workflow that predates `--config`, which is what makes the "`schema` stays 1" of the same fact honest rather than merely additive. **(2) The old selection was two methods, which is why listing did not change.** `Filters` is read at exactly `admits(group, name)` and `packages()`, so the new selection is a **superset of those two methods** and `mirror/source.rs` changed by rename alone — no second listing path — while `all`, the excludes, the `[[template]]` rows and the payload plan ride beside them. **(3) An empty axis cannot mean two things.** `Filters` reads "no packages and no groups" as "everything", which is right for a flag nobody passed and wrong under `[select]`: a configuration whose only content is `[[template]]` rows would have selected the whole source. With neither ordinary axis naming anything, only the template rows select; a run with no selection at all never reaches that rule, because it is `all` from the start. **(4) The target is read before the source is listed.** The recorded selection lives inside the target’s own tree and decides what the source is asked for, so `read_target` moved ahead of the listing stage — for a `monorepo`, the same shallow fetch one stage earlier. **(5) `WRITER_DIRS` must *not* learn `templates`, and `repomd.json` is not touched at all.** `#MIRROR-SNAPSHOT-LAYOUT`’s last sentence asks for both. `WRITER_DIRS` (`crates/vibe-index/src/index/mod.rs`) is the whitelist of what `Index::write_to` itself **produces**, read by `rebuild.rs` `catalog_file_set` and `index/memory/projection_compare.rs` `projection_matches`; the mirror writes the snapshot through `BatchConfig.files`, so `_index/templates/` stays outside that whitelist exactly as `README.md`, `.gitignore` and `state/` do, and teaching it otherwise would make the projection comparison expect a tree the writer never writes. The `repomd.json` `files` key is withdrawn by the owner-facing session (AV-FMT-010): the snapshot lives at a fixed path a client already knows, and a new first-class input to the index’s own manifest is out of this phase’s scope. **(6) The `Stale` risk the plan carried does not exist.** `listing.txt` is `render_listing(version_dirs, journal_digest)` (`crates/vibe-core/src/layout_registry.rs`) and `version_dirs` skips `_index` altogether, so a snapshot directory cannot move the listing; the obligation is replaced by one test that a registry which grows `_index/templates/` still reads `Fresh`. **(7) `BatchConfig` gains a removal channel** (commit (c)): prune’s deletion, the index rewrite and the journal facts — `Event::Removed` already exists — must land in ONE commit, which is what `#MIRROR-PRUNE`’s "rewritten in the same commit as the removal" requires and which the existing `files`-only channel cannot express. **(8) A snapshot needs a directory-shaped source.** `TemplateLayer::for_directory` is what reads a template out of a registry, so a `[[template]]` row against a per-package Git source is refused **by name** before anything is listed or written, the limitation `#TEMPLATE-DISCOVERY` already states. **(9) `versions.json`’s `sha256` is recomputed.** The envelope `#TEMPLATE-CACHE` defines is `CachedVersionList { source_url, sha256, fetched_at, document }`, and `#MIRROR-SNAPSHOT-LAYOUT` restricts `document` to the selected versions — so the digest must be taken over the **filtered** document, never carried over from the upstream fetch, or a client would read a hash of bytes it does not have. **(10) Three refusals the design did not name**, each a declaration that cannot mean what it says: `newest = 0` keeps no version of any major, `[payloads] max_total = 0` admits no payload at all, and two `[[template]]` rows for one package. They join the refusals the fact does name. **(11) The snapshot layout lives in one place, and priming is the whole client mechanism.** `#MIRROR-TEMPLATE-SNAPSHOT` asks that a client inside a closed network render «with the same code as outside». As built the layout, the record type and the filtered envelope are one module in `vibe-registry` that the mirror writes and the client reads, and the client half is a single act: discovering a template in a directory registry **primes this machine's template cache** from the registry's snapshot, after which the version-list and digest readers find an ordinary cache hit and never reach the transport. So the claim is literal rather than careful — there is no second reader to disagree, and no reader below discovery learns that the bytes came from a registry. **(12) A broken snapshot reads as absent, never as a refusal.** A snapshot is a cache of someone else's bytes, so a wrong `schema`, an unparseable record, a `versions.json` whose `sha256` does not hash its own `document`, and a `[[version]]` row whose digest file is missing or does not hash to it each leave the client with its own cache and whatever network it has. A refusal would make the whole registry unusable for every package, including the ones with no template at all. Each reason is warned about where it is detected, so a broken snapshot is degraded and never silent. **(13) Priming never overwrites a cache entry that is already there.** A digest document of a released version is immutable, so a local copy and a snapshot copy of one version cannot honestly differ — and if they did, overwriting would erase exactly the evidence the alarm of `#TEMPLATE-LOCK-RECORD` exists to raise. **(14) `versions.json`'s `sha256` is recomputed over the filtered document, and a reader checks it.** Amendment 9 states the writer's obligation; as built the reader enforces it, because an envelope whose hash does not describe the bytes beside it would put those bytes in the cache under a provenance that is not theirs. **(15) A row's `platforms` / `archs` / `installers` do not change the snapshot.** A snapshot carries a version's *inputs* — its version record and its digest document — which are per version and not per installer option, so those keys are reported and otherwise inert until payload projection acts on them in (c). **(16) `versions` and `channels` on one row are a union, not an intersection.** `#MIRROR-CONFIG-SCHEMA` lists both without saying how they compose. As built `versions = [">=24"]` with `channels = ["lts"]` means «everything from 24 up, and the LTS line whatever its number», which is what an operator supplying a closed network wants; an intersection would silently drop the older LTS releases that are the reason to name a channel at all. `newest = N` then applies per major to that union, which is what «after the other filters» means. **(17) The removal channel's order is delete-then-reproject, and its path is validated against the coordinate it claims.** Amendment 4 said `BatchConfig` needs a removal channel so that `#MIRROR-PRUNE`'s «rewritten in the same commit as the removal» holds; building it settled three things the fact leaves implicit. First, the journal fact alone does not drop a version: `vibe_index::layout::refresh` projects the catalog from the **tree** (`layout::version_dirs`), so a directory still on disk when the index is rewritten is projected straight back in — the deletion must happen before the re-projection, inside the same `write_index` call, which is precisely why this is a batch channel and not a step beside the batch. Second, a `monorepo` must **stage** the deleted paths: `commit_batch` stages a computed list, and a deletion missing from it leaves the working tree without the file and the pushed commit with it, so the registry would go on advertising bytes it no longer has while every local check passed. Third, the channel carries a path *and* the `(group, name, version)` whose fact it implies, and those can disagree — so the path must spell the coordinate exactly, a path that is neither a version directory nor inside `_index/` is refused outright (a batch has no business deleting the rest of the tree and the mistake is unrecoverable), and every refusal lands before anything is deleted. A path the tree does **not** hold is dropped rather than refused, because a prune plan is read against one state and applied against a possibly newer one, and a version someone else already removed is the outcome asked for. `#MIRROR-NO-SILENT-PRUNE` is unaffected and holds by construction while nothing asks to prune: the mirror passes an empty channel, and `--prune` fills it only after its plan has been answered. **(18) A projected payload is the installer’s own fetch with a destination the caller chooses.** `#MIRROR-PAYLOAD-PROJECTION` says the mirror «fetches each one through the operation’s controlled transport, verifies it against the digest the render produced, and writes it into the drop». As built that is not a second reader: the one public entry `vibe_app::fetch_declared_input` wraps the installer's existing Locator fetch, so the remapped candidates are tried in winning order, the digest is verified on whichever served the bytes, and every HTTP download is journaled by the one transfer wrapper `PROP-068#coverage` requires — the mirror adds no reader of its own and is therefore not a new line in that gate’s exemption list. Each input is written under a scratch name in the destination's own directory and renamed into place, so a partial file is never left where the drop lookup reads. **(19) Only a URL input is projectable, and the drop rung is computed, not invented.** A package-relative `source` is already inside the package the mirror copies, and an input declared `drop = "packages"` is one an administrator places by hand — which is what projection is doing — so both are skipped rather than refused. The destination is `[payloads] into` joined with the coordinate and the URL’s last segment, and a unit test asserts it equals `package_lookup`'s first rung for that coordinate and file name, rather than restating the convention here. **(20) The projection reads the renders the snapshot stage already performed.** A full render costs a digest document and a substitution, and `#MIRROR-PAYLOAD-PROJECTION` asks that each selected version be «rendered fully» — which the snapshot stage does anyway. So the stage keeps its renders, but **only for a row with `payloads = true`**: a four-hundred-version selection must not hold four hundred manifests for a row that asked for no payload. The installer options a row keeps are then resolved against the *rendered* manifest, where `installers` names them outright and wins over `platforms` / `archs`, as `#MIRROR-CONFIG-SCHEMA` says. **(21) The per-row facts had to become a carrier, and the row’s human form had to move.** Commit (b) deliberately reported a template row where it was produced and carried nothing out, on the ground that the only reader was the human form. Two readers arrived together — the projection, which needs the renders, and `#FORMAT-CHANGES`’ AV-FMT-009 `templates[]`, which needs the counts — and a row must be drawn **once**, with its bytes. So the snapshot stage answers with its outcomes and draws nothing, and both answers are produced beside the projection, which is the one place every fact of a row comes together. **(22) An unanswered prune plan refuses the whole run.** `#MIRROR-PRUNE` says «nothing is removed without `--yes`», which would also be satisfied by copying and not pruning. As built an unattended run without `--yes` refuses with `prune_consent_required` and writes nothing at all, because a plan is read against **one** reading of the target and applied against a possibly newer one: a run that printed a plan and then changed the very tree it described would have printed a document about nothing. An attended run asks, through the same prompt machinery PROP-066 `#consent` uses, and a no refuses the same way. `--dry-run --prune` prints the plan and stops, successfully. **(23) `--prune` needs a *declared* selection, and says so.** It removes what the **recorded** selection no longer matches, and amendment 1 is why `--package` / `--group` are never recorded: they are a per-run override whose second job is making an unlistable source mirrorable one package at a time. Pruning by one would delete what the operator’s own declaration still asks for, so a flag-selected run refuses by name, and so do `--prune-payloads` without `--prune` and `--prune-payloads` with no row that asks for payloads — the drop it would empty is named by the configuration that filled it. **(24) A removal takes the version directory, and an emptied `<group>/<name>/` stays.** The channel of amendment 17 refuses any path that is not a version directory or inside `_index/`, which is what keeps a batch from deleting the rest of the tree; a parent left empty carries no version, no catalog row and no journal fact, so it is the harmless side of that refusal rather than something to work around by widening the channel. On a `monorepo` it is not even visible, because git tracks no empty directory. **(25) The drop is emptied after the commit, and it is the only removal outside the batch.** A registry that has stopped advertising bytes it still holds is safe; one that advertises bytes it no longer holds is not. So `--prune-payloads` removes its directories once the batch has been committed, and a batch that failed leaves the drop as it was. **(26) A snapshot’s prune is decided where the snapshot is written.** Dropping a version from a snapshot means three consistent changes: the digest file goes, `snapshot.toml` loses its `[[version]]` row, and `versions.json` is re-filtered with its `sha256` recomputed over the new bytes (amendments 9 and 14). Computing that anywhere but the writer would duplicate the record-writing logic, so the stage keeps only the selected versions when a prune is asked for, and the plan is built from the stale set it reports. The digest files ride the removal channel as `_index/` paths with no coordinate, which is exactly what a removal without a version is for. **(27) A snapshot the selection names no `[[template]]` row for goes whole.** It is reported with its own reason rather than lumped in with a narrowed row, because the two are different operator mistakes — one narrowed a row, the other stopped declaring the template at all — and the second also empties that package’s whole payload directory in the drop. A snapshot directory whose group id this vibe cannot parse is left alone: an unreadable name is never a reason to delete.

p.P7A-AS-BUILT: **Implemented 2026-11-10 (campaign phase P7a) — what the code decided that `#VERSION-FILE-KEYED` and `#VERSION-FILE-WRITE` left open.** Seven amendments, and the first two are the ones a later pass would otherwise re-derive. **(1) The short spelling is sugar in **both** directions, which is what makes "byte-for-byte" true rather than nearly true.** The fact says `tool-versions` expands into one `keyed` row before anything reads a file, and that is how it is built: `VersionFileDecl` has exactly two variants, `Plain` and `Keyed`, and the authored `format = "tool-versions"` lowers into `Keyed` in the deserialiser, so there is one reader, one writer and one validator. The fact does not say what happens on the way **out**, and a one-way expansion would have rewritten the real packages' manifests and every derived sidecar into the long form on the next write. So the conversion back is the same rule read the other way: a `Keyed` row that is *exactly* `names = [".tool-versions"]`, `separator = "whitespace"`, `comment = "hash"`, `extra = "first"` serialises as `format = "tool-versions"` again. It is a pure function of the row — nothing remembers which spelling an author used — so the two cannot drift, and `format()` answers `"tool-versions"` for such a row, which is also what keeps the sidecar's existing documents byte-identical. **(2) The three closed vocabularies are refused by *us*, not by serde, because serde cannot name a TOML path.** The fact requires each refusal to name its TOML path (PROP-059 `#declaration`). Measured: an unknown enum variant inside `[[application.version_file]]` comes out of `toml` as «unknown variant `tabs`, expected one of …, in `application.version_file` at line 11» — the *table* and the line, never the member. So `separator` / `comment` / `extra` arrive as text and are lowered row by row, and each refusal reads `application.version_file[0].separator: ...` with the vocabulary listed. The two fields a `keyed` row cannot omit (`key`, `separator`) are refused the same way rather than as serde's «missing field», for the same reason. **(3) A `keyed` row's file-name refusals name `format` when the row is the short spelling.** A row authored as `tool-versions` has no `names` array to name, so the field a refusal quotes is decided from the row's own shape — `format` for the sugar shape, `names` otherwise — which keeps every pre-existing `tool-versions` refusal message exactly as it was. **(4) The sidecar's wire gains a `keyed` mapping; `AV-FMT-025`'s "no wire change" was half right.** `vibe-app-version-files/1` carries a declared row as declared, and a genuinely `keyed` row has five fields the document had no shape for. The mapping is added (epoch **1 → 1**, three closed vocabularies), and because the sugar round-trips, a home whose packages declare only `.tool-versions` writes the document it wrote before, byte for byte. A row whose vocabulary word this build does not know is read as unknown history, the posture the sidecar already took for an unreadable document. **(5) `extra = "refuse"` makes the line a reported fault, and the search walks on.** The fact calls such a line «a reported, unusable line» without saying what the search then does. As built it is exactly what an unparseable `plain` line already is: a fault in the report and no selection, so the upward walk continues and a prompt hook cannot fail a `cd`. **(6) A keyed write preserves the line's trailing comment as well as its spacing.** The fact names the separator and the spacing; a line like `maven = 3.9.9 # pinned` also carries a comment, and rewriting only the value region keeps it. The implementation splits a line into head (indent, key, separator, the spacing after it), values and tail (the spacing and the comment), replaces the values and writes the two ends back unchanged — and the line ending is the line's own, because the rewrite never goes through a parser. A created or appended line is spelled `key=value`, `key value` or `key: value`, one spelling per separator. **(7) The flag is reported in the documents the two commands already emit, and refused everywhere it would be ignored.** `AV-FMT-019` says `--json` carries the path and the version; as built that is one optional member on `vibe-application-command-report/2` (`versionFile`) and one on `vibe-app-alternatives/1` (`version_file`), both epoch **1 → 1** and both absent unless a file was written. `--write-version-file` is a usage refusal naming the flag on a project install, a remap package, a global MCP package, `--plan-only` (which resolves a version and installs none) and `vibe app use --none` (a slot that is off resolves to no version), rather than a flag that is silently ignored. The write runs **after** the command has settled, so the version written is the one the slot now resolves to, and the resolution cache of the edited directory is dropped. **One premise of the plan's own risk list did not hold:** the risk note says the real Node package declares `tool-versions`, and at `240b8abaa` neither `org.vibevm.node/node` nor anything else in the tree declares any `[[application.version_file]]` row at all, so the compatibility of the short spelling is proved by tests rather than observed on a shipped package.

p.P6-AS-BUILT: **Implemented 2026-11-10 (campaign phase P6) — what the code decided that the design left open or stated differently.** Ten amendments, each a consequence of the actual tree rather than a change of intent. **(1) A migration step is literally a `StepDecl`.** `#MIGRATION-DECLARATION` says each side is "exactly one step declaration of the existing `StepDecl` grammar", and as built it is: `id` and `title` are required of it like of any step, and the runner uses them for the record, the progress row and the log file name. Synthesising them from the entry would have meant either loosening `StepDecl` for every installer option or reading the table twice; the small verbosity buys a grammar with no second spelling. **(2) Four fields are refused, not ignored.** A migration step that declares `requires`, `when`, `unless` or a non-default `phase` is a validation refusal naming the field, because the migration runner has no requirement resolution (its PATH is the two installations’, by construction), no feature or parameter selection to evaluate a condition against, and no prepare/finish split. Admitting them would have meant silently ignoring an author’s declaration, which `PROP-059#declaration` forbids. **(3) `--registry DIR` joins the spelling.** A migration step is the package’s own script, and the inventory does not retain a package tree, so `vibe app migrate` resolves **both** versions through the ordinary registry chain exactly as `vibe app modify` does — and therefore takes the same resolution flag every other package-reading `app` subcommand has. The refusal when a tree cannot be reached is `migration_unresolvable`, before any effect. **(4) The report is the record.** `#MIGRATION-FAILURE` describes a report and a resumable work directory; as built they are one document, `vibe-app-migration/1` written as `<work>/migration.json` after every side. That is what `--resume` reads to re-run only the import, and it means one registered format instead of two. A corrupt record is no record and costs one re-run, never an error. **(5) The consent code is `migration_consent_required`.** `#MIGRATION-FAILURE` names the refusal `consent_required`; that code was already taken by `AgentError::ConsentRequired` (PROP-064), and the codes of this subsystem are globally unique by construction (`every_code_is_unique_snake_case_and_explained`). The class (`Refusal`, exit 2), the message and the exact printed command are as specified. **(6) The logs live one level down.** The shared work directory’s top level belongs entirely to the package’s scripts, so an entry’s two logs are `<work>/logs/<entry id>/export.log` and `import.log`. The first version put them at `<work>/<entry id>/`, and the CLI fixture caught the collision immediately: an entry called `second` could not write a file called `second`. **(7) `--resume` reuses the newest run of the pair.** The work directory is `<home>/cache/app-migrate/<slot>/<from>-to-<to>/<timestamp>/` as specified, which leaves "which one" open: a fresh run always takes a new timestamp, because the previous directory is evidence and is never replaced, and `--resume` takes the newest kept one, refusing `nothing_to_resume` when there is none. Every slot and version component is sanitised to one portable file name, so no declaration can reach out of the migration root. **(8) `/7` retains the declared entries too.** `#FORMAT-CHANGES`’ AV-FMT-017 moves the `Installation` record to `vibe-user-applications/7` for the template provenance and the migration outcomes; as built it also retains the **declared** entries (`id`, `name`, `description`, `default`). Without them the offer after `vibe app use` could not exist at all — that command resolves no package — and `--only ID` would need a registry to validate a typo. They ride in the same move rather than forcing a second one. The template provenance is read at publication time off this invocation’s template layer (`vibe_registry::templates::active()`’s note for the exact resolved version), so P2’s amendment (3) stands and `ResolvedPackage` still grows no field. **(9) The version-file sidecar stays beside the index.** The `/7` move reopens AV-FMT-101’s question and the answer is unchanged: the sidecar is `recoverable = true` derived state while the index is `recoverable = false`, and folding it in would cost the writer a rung of its ladder — a home that declares a version file but retains no template provenance and no migration record writes `/6` today and would be forced to `/7`, which needs the proxy admission `PROP-059#proxy-index-upgrade` requires, for no fact the home does not already hold. **(10) The ordinary engine, named precisely.** `#MIGRATION-DECLARATION` says both sides run through “the step runner, the interpreters, `needs`, the display panel of `#display`, the cancellation of `#cancellation` and the run records of `#runs`”. The step runner, the interpreters, `needs` and cancellation are literal: the per-step entry point of `PROP-065#kinds` is what runs each side, an unmet `needs` row refuses before the child starts so the entry has changed nothing, and the caller’s interrupt reaches the child through the same `ChildIo`. Two are substituted, deliberately: a migration draws the **flat** display rather than the step panel, because two steps per entry do not make a panel; and it writes no `app-runs` record, because a `RunRecord` is keyed to an installation and one of four `Command` verbs. Its evidence is the always-kept work directory — the per-side logs plus the `vibe-app-migration/1` record — which is strictly stronger than `#runs`, whose records `vibe app runs --prune` may delete.

p.P7B-AS-BUILT: **Implemented 2026-11-10 (campaign phase P7b) — what the code decided that `#ECOSYSTEM-ADAPTER`, `#ECOSYSTEM-RECOMMENDS` and `#ECOSYSTEM-MIGRATION` left open, and the two clauses that are deliberately **not** built.** Twelve amendments. **(1) The recommends shorthand is sugar in both directions, which is what keeps the feature fixed point untouched.** `#ECOSYSTEM-RECOMMENDS` says each row synthesises one `[[installer_options.features]]` row in every option, and says nothing about the way out. A one-way synthesis would have written those rows into the document the next time a manifest was serialised — `vibe init` does serialise one — and the next parse would then have refused them as colliding with themselves. So the rows are put in by `TryFrom<ManifestWire> for Manifest` and taken out again by `TryFrom<Manifest> for ManifestWire`, and `FeatureDecl` carries one never-authored, never-serialised `origin` marker (`authored`, or the recommends shorthand) to tell them apart — the device `StepDecl.origin` and `LauncherDecl.source` already are. Doing it in the wire conversion rather than in a dozen readers is what makes the row **ordinary in every respect**: the resolution of PROP-065 `#feature-tree`, `--feature` / `--no-feature`, the attended multi-select, the profiles and the recorded chosen set all see it as authored, and the existing feature-tree suite passes unchanged, which was the phase's stated regression gate. **(2) One pre-existing refusal had to be narrowed, and only one.** `[[installer_options]]` refuses `features` on a **method-form** option (an option with `installation` and no `steps`), and a recommendation reaches every option, method-form ones included, because it is a property of the package and not of one platform's archive. That refusal now reads the author's own rows only, so an author who writes `features` on a method option is refused exactly as before and the synthesised row passes. **(3) A recommends row's `ecosystem` field is what routes the item.** The row is authored inside an `[[application.ecosystem]]` table, so the field looks redundant; the fact nevertheless requires it and requires an unknown id to be refused by name. As built, the field is authoritative: a row belongs to the adapter it names, which must be one the package declares, and a row naming a *different* declared adapter is admitted. **(4) A duplicate recommendation id is a refusal too**, naming its path: each row synthesises one feature of that id, so two rows of one id could not both be it. **(5) The reserved-namespace refusal must come first.** `ecosystem:npm` is not a portable token — a colon is not a token character — so the pre-existing «must be a portable lowercase token» refusal would have fired first and never mentioned the reserved namespace the author actually tripped over. The prefix is therefore tested before the token shape. **(6) The synthesised migration entry is a pure function of the adapter**, `EcosystemDecl::migration_entry()`: `Some` when the adapter declares a `list` verb and does not set `migration = false`, with the `list` verb as the export, the `install` verb as the import, the adapter's name, and `default = true`. `ApplicationDecl::migration_entries()` is the one reader of both spellings — the authored rows, then the synthesised ones — and the installation record is built from it, so `migration_plan`, the post-install offer and a later `--only ecosystem:<id>` need no package tree, exactly as an authored id does not. **(7) The ordinary migration runner grew one input, not a second runner.** A synthesised entry's two sides are adapter verbs, so `StepContext` carries an ecosystem environment **beside** the migration one: the export runs the `list` verb with `VIBE_ECOSYSTEM_LIST` pointing into the shared work directory, and the import runs the `install` verb with exactly the lines that file holds as its argv. The items travel in `<work>/logs/ecosystem-<id>/items`, and that directory name replaces the reserved `ecosystem:` prefix with `ecosystem-` because a colon is not a portable path component; an authored id is a portable token and so is unchanged. **(8) The work directory is per version, not per adapter**, as `#ECOSYSTEM-ADAPTER` spells it, so one invocation that touches several adapters writes **one** `vibe-app-ecosystem/1` document with one `adapters[]` row each — the adapter id, the items asked for verbatim, the observation, the outcome, the step, its log and the retry command — and the slot, the installation key, the verb and the directory on the document itself. The outcome vocabulary is `done | failed | skipped`; `skipped` is an adapter that declares no such verb, or one whose item list was empty, and is never an error. Its `vibe app work` key is `ecosystem:<slot>:<version>:<verb>`. **(9) A named adapter refuses, an unnamed one skips.** `--ecosystem ID` naming an adapter the package does not declare, or one that declares no such verb, is a refusal naming what it does declare; with no `--ecosystem` the same shape is reported `skipped`, because only `install` is required of an adapter and asking every one of them about `self_upgrade` is not a mistake. **(10) An adapter verb sees `VIBE_APP_ROOT`.** `AV-FMT-026` names the four `VIBE_ECOSYSTEM_*` variables «beside the ones PROP-065 `#templates` passes» and states that `VIBE_OUT` is not set. As built the verb also gets `VIBE_APP_ROOT` — the one installation it configures, which is the whole point of the verb — while `VIBE_OUT` and `VIBE_SOURCES` are removed and `$out` is unexpandable, exactly as for a migration side. A *migration* side of a synthesised entry keeps the migration environment's own rule and sees `VIBE_FROM_APP_ROOT` / `VIBE_TO_APP_ROOT` instead. **(11) `vibe app describe`'s adapters are on the `application` object** — the declaration's own place in the document — and carry declaration only: id, name, description, the `migration` flag, the verbs declared, and the recommendations with their items. The *last applied* and *last observed* lists the fact promises there come from the installation record, which is (12). **(12) The two clauses this phase did not build, and why they are not P7b's.** The **per-adapter installation record** — the last applied and last observed list with their times — is `AV-FMT-029`, which the plan assigns to P7c together with the `[format.application-index]` **6 → 7** move, the `vibe-user-applications/8` tag and the `vibe-app-proxy` admission PROP-059 `#proxy-index-upgrade` requires. P7b therefore leaves the inventory at `/7` and **does not** move the generation: nothing it retains is new state, because the synthesised migration entries go into the `migrations` list that generation already carries. (**Paid by P7d on 2026-11-10**, which landed first: the `e7` schema, the `/8` tag, the frozen `/7` reader and the proxy admission are in, so P7c adds its per-adapter record as optional members of that same generation at epoch 7 → 7 — `PROP-077#P7D-AS-BUILT` (1).) The user's own list (`[slot.<slot>.extras.<ecosystem>]`), the final-list arithmetic over it, `vibe app extras apply|add|drop|import`, the apply after `install -g` and `--no-extras` are `#SLOT-EXTRAS`' own and stay P7c's; what landed here is the half that needs no user list — `extras list`, `remove` and `self-upgrade`, each acting on the version the slot's default points at, because the fact gives those commands no version argument. `extras list` runs the `list` verb and keeps answering when it fails, naming why in `observed_failed`: a listing that refused to say what it does know would be the wrong trade.

p.P7C-AS-BUILT: **Implemented 2026-11-10 (campaign phase P7c) — what the code decided that `#SLOT-EXTRAS` left open, and the two clauses it closed on `#ECOSYSTEM-ADAPTER`.** Eleven amendments. **(1) The `vibe-app` → user-config seam is a path threaded in, not an ambient read.** The owner put the list in the user's own settings and the plan called that seam the phase's real architectural cost. As built the cost is paid where the plan said — `crates/vibe-app/` reads and interprets `UserConfig`, which it never did before — but the *path* arrives on `OperationContext` from the caller, because this crate's own standing rule is that it reads no environment: the one chokepoint that resolves `$VIBE_SETTINGS` / `VIBEVM_USER_CONFIG` into a file stays in `vibe-cli`, beside the PATH and agent facts it already gathers. The gain is not tidiness: a context with no path behaves **exactly** as a home with no `[slot]` table, so the "unchanged for everyone else" property the plan demanded a test for is structural rather than careful, and no test can reach the operator's real `config.toml` by forgetting something. **(2) A `config.toml` that will not parse is a notice, not a refusal.** The fact makes a stale *line* non-fatal and says nothing about a file that will not parse at all. "Failure never touches the runtime" decides it: an unreadable file is one notice and an empty list, never a failed install. Nothing is hidden by that — a malformed user config is already reported by the startup read every command performs. **(3) The listing answers the same arithmetic under the same flags.** `#SLOT-EXTRAS` gives `extras list` no flags and the P7b half computed only the author's enabled rows. As built `list` takes `--no-extras`, honours the global `--no-recommends`, and its computed list **is** the final list, so `vibe app extras list SLOT --no-extras` is an honest preview of `vibe app extras apply SLOT --no-extras` instead of a second opinion. `--no-recommends`' usage admission therefore widened to `app extras list|apply`, and to those two verbs only: on `remove` and `self-upgrade` the flag would decide nothing, and PROP-077 `#NO-RECOMMENDS-FLAG`'s own rule is that a flag silently ignored is worse than a flag refused. **(4) `add` / `drop` / `import` take the slot first, and infer the ecosystem.** The fact spells the editors `add ITEM…` / `drop ID…` with no slot, which cannot address a table keyed by slot **and** ecosystem; every verb of the family therefore takes `SLOT` first, as the other four already did. `--ecosystem` stays optional, because the nvm case the fact names (`vibe app extras import node ~/.nvm/default-packages`) reads badly with it: the user's own file decides when it already holds exactly one ecosystem for that slot — so a second edit of an existing list needs no package tree, no registry and no network — else the slot's current version decides when it declares exactly one, else the command refuses naming what there is. Ambiguity is never guessed. **(5) "Placed a new version" is measured as a key the home did not hold.** The fact says the apply follows an install that placed a new version and explicitly not a reinstall of one already installed. As built the condition is the set of installation keys captured **before** the operation: `install -g`, `update -g` and `update -g --all` each apply when they commit a key that was absent. The request then names *that key* rather than the slot, because the slot's default is the user's to move and an install need not have moved it — a `--hidden` install of a second version gets its own extras in its own version. **(6) The same call is a warning after an install and an exit status when typed.** `vibe app extras apply` is a command the user asked for, so its exit status follows the run. The identical call made after an install reports and returns nothing: the version stays installed, the slot default stays put and the install's own status is untouched. A package declaring no ecosystem adapter at all — the great majority of applications — is silent rather than warned about, and that one refusal is recognised by its error **code**, never by its prose. **(7) The record is per adapter, and a skip writes nothing.** An apply records the list it **asked for** with its time and outcome, which is what makes a failed apply still answerable; a `list` records what it observed; a failed observation leaves the previous list standing and names itself in its own outcome, because a lost observation costs one re-run and never a wrong answer; and `remove` / `self_upgrade` change what a version carries without being an apply, so they do not rewrite the applied list — only a fresh `list` can say what is there now. A `skipped` adapter writes nothing at all, so the writer and `Index::requires_reader_eight` agree on exactly one question ("does this record retain anything?") and an adapter that only ever skipped cannot push a home onto a reader its PATH proxies may not have. **(8) A recommendation is routed by its `ecosystem` field here too, which fixed a delivered defect.** `#P7B-AS-BUILT` (3) settled that the field is authoritative and that a row naming a *different* declared adapter is admitted; the delivered listing nevertheless read `EcosystemDecl::recommends` — the rows as authored — so such a row's item would have been handed to the wrong adapter's `install` verb. `ApplicationDecl::ecosystem_recommends_of` is now the single reader, and the final list and the listing share it. **(9) `dropped` is a member of its own.** A recommendation the user dropped is not an unchosen one: the two are different acts, and only one of them is reversible with `--feature`. The listing therefore carries `dropped` beside `enabled` rather than making `enabled` lie, and the human report marks the three states apart. **(10) The `describe` half carries times as well as lists.** `AV-FMT-032` promises the last applied and last observed **lists**; as built each carries its RFC 3339 time too, because a list with no date cannot tell a reader whether it is describing this version's history or a stale record, and the inventory already holds both. `describe` still runs nothing: it is declaration plus retained record. **(11) The generation was inherited finished, exactly as promised.** `PROP-077#P7D-AS-BUILT` (1) said P7d had paid the `e7` schema, the `vibe-user-applications/8` tag, the frozen `/7` reader and the `vibe-app-proxy` admission. It had: the per-adapter record went in as **optional members of that same generation at epoch 7 → 7**, costing one clause in `Index::requires_reader_eight` and one in the reader's generation guard, with no new generation, no new protocol tag and no second proxy admission.

p.P7F-AS-BUILT: **Implemented 2026-11-11 (campaign phase P7f, the shim half) — what building `org.vibevm.node/vibenvm` and running the proof against it decided.** Eleven amendments. **(1) Every version a target names is spelled `=<version>`, and this is the sharpest thing the differential caught.** nvm's `22.9.0` is *one release*; vibe's `@22.9.0` is a *requirement*, so against the suite's pinned set `vibe install -g org.vibevm.node/node@22.9.0` installed **22.11.0** and `vibe app exec node@22.9.0 -- node -v` ran 22.11.0. The shim therefore translates nvm's prefix match by counting the fields the user typed — `22.9.0` → `=22.9.0`, `22.9` → `~22.9`, `22` → `22`, `node`/`stable` → `latest`, `lts` and `lts/*` → `lts`, `lts/jod` → `lts/jod` — and that table is the only translation it carries. Everything else a user types is handed to vibe as written, so a vibe requirement (`^22`, `>=20 <23`) works too. The same `=` spelling had to reach the suite's own observer, which was reading one version's global packages with a requirement and would have silently observed another. **(2) The shim holds no state and no version logic, and that is checkable rather than claimed.** One file, one public function `nvm`, helpers in the reserved `__vibenvm_` namespace, nothing written and nothing cached: every version is resolved by `vibe app env --use` (installed) or `vibe install -g … --plan-only --json` (available), every install is `vibe install -g`, every activation is `vibe app env`, every listing is `vibe app versions`, and what a `.nvmrc` says is read by `vibe app env --project --json` and never by the shim. `nvm unload` unsets the function, its helpers and its three variables. **(3) Three vibe surfaces answered what the shim needed, each a declared document rather than human text.** `vibe-app-env/1`'s `version_file` selection carries `requested` whether or not that version is installed, which is what a bare `nvm install` needs; `vibe-app-plan/1`'s `package.version` resolves a requirement against everything the registries and the template offer while downloading nothing, which is `nvm version-remote`; and `vibe-app-list/1` is the home's own inventory, needing no registry, no template and no request, which is what the suite's `installed` and `default` observations read. **(4) Four shortfalls found and reported, none patched in the shim** (the VIBENVM rule): `vibe install -g` with no version does not consult the declared version file, so the shim composes `app env --project` and an install; `vibe app versions` has no version-pattern filter, so `nvm ls <pattern>` / `ls-remote <pattern>` answer with the one version the requirement resolves to; `--write-version-file` lives only on `install -g` and `app use`, so `nvm use --save` moves the slot default as a side effect nvm does not have; and a version file's bare `22.9.0` reads as a caret requirement, so a written `.nvmrc` stops pinning what it recorded once a newer minor is installed. **(5) nvm's exit statuses are part of the surface, and "nothing matched" is 3.** `ls`, `ls-remote`, `version`, `version-remote` and `which` print `N/A` and exit 3 when nothing is selected, where vibe refuses an unknown slot with 2 and lists happily otherwise. The shim maps that status, which is translation and not behaviour; the twelve owner-approved refusals exit **55**, nvm's own status for an unsupported option, each printing the owner's reason. **(6) The two best-effort npm verbs, and the question their exit status answers.** nvm's `install-latest-npm` ends in an echo, so a failed `npm install -g npm` leaves it exiting 0. The Node package's `self_upgrade` script does not copy that by accident: it asks the newest npm *this node line* can run (upstream's own ceilings, because `npm@latest` on an older runtime installs an npm that cannot start), attempts it, and then answers the question **"does this installation have a usable package manager"** rather than "was the network up" — succeeding with a notice when the attempt could not be made and npm still runs, failing when npm does not run. Measured in the sandbox: npm reports `E404` against the loopback registry and both tools exit 0 having changed nothing. **(7) The adapter's `list` leaves out `npm` and `corepack`, and that decision is what makes the two carry verbs agree.** Both live inside every Node distribution's own `lib/node_modules`: they are the runtime's managers, not packages anybody added, and carrying them into another version would overwrite that version's own bundled pair with one upstream never tested it against. Found by a mismatch: with corepack in the list, `vibe app migrate … --only ecosystem:npm` carried a bundled manager, failed against the loopback registry and exited 1, while nvm — whose own list excludes npm and predates corepack — swallowed the identical failure and exited 0. **(8) The shim finds `vibe` on PATH, as a user has it, and carries no test-only variable.** The suite gives sandbox B the binary in a directory of its own, deliberately **outside** the tool root so it never appears in the `owned_path` observation, and declares the local registry as that home's own `[[registry]]` (`type = "localdir"`, a `file://` url) rather than passing `--registry` on one command — because the shim calls `vibe install -g org.vibevm.node/node@…` exactly as a user's shell would. **(9) Three of the suite's own comparisons had to be made resolved rather than stored, and one normalisation had to be widened.** `default` follows nvm's alias chain as `nvm_resolve_alias` does and reports `absent` when what it lands on is not installed, because nvm's `default` survives the uninstall of the version it names and a default naming a version that is gone provides nothing; `aliases` reports what each name resolves to, with vibe's `lts` under nvm's spelling `lts/*`, and asks for the channels **offline** so the observation makes no request of its own and reports only what the tool has already fetched — which is exactly what nvm's alias store is; and the `<TOOLROOT>@v<version>` collapse did **not** cover vibe's layout as the harness half hoped, because it required the version to be a path component (`versions/node/v22.9.0`) while vibe's is the version half of a coordinate (`apps/node/org.vibevm.node.node@22.9.0`). A second rule drops a leading `v` from a version that starts a field or a member of one, because nvm writes `v22.9.0` where vibe writes `22.9.0` and nvm's own `nvm_version` adds and strips it freely. **(10) One case's two whole-list spellings name nvm's own `node` flavour.** A bare `nvm ls-remote` lists "node AND io.js" and returns the io.js half's status, which against the suite's empty loopback io.js mirror is 3 — so a required pair's exit status would have been decided entirely by nvm's io.js category, which is an owner-approved accepted gap vibe has no concept of at all. Naming the flavour keeps the observable inside the surface both tools have and covers the same pair, because the coverage gate reads flags only from the tokens directly after the subcommand. **(11) The Node package's additions are a new template revision, 1.1.0, and the hand-written migration entry the plan expected to drop did not exist.** The byte-for-byte golden gate renders the frozen 1.0.0 copy of the template against the two concretely published manifests, so adding the adapter and the version files at 1.0.0 would have broken it; the fixture tracks 1.0.0 deliberately and a newer revision is a new fixture, never an edit of that one. And at 1.0.0 the package declared no `[[application.migration]]` at all, so `#ECOSYSTEM-MIGRATION`'s "drops its hand-written `npm-globals` migration entry" is satisfied vacuously: the synthesised `ecosystem:npm` is the only entry the package has ever had.

p.P7-CLOSE-AS-BUILT: **Implemented 2026-11-11 (the campaign's close-out) — the four shortfalls P7f found, closed as one design, and the whole-campaign acceptance script.** Seven things a later session would otherwise re-derive. **(1) One rule answered all four rows, and that is why they were not four patches.** `B-262`…`B-265` read as four gaps and are one: *what does a spelling that names versions mean, and where*. The answer is `#VERSION-FILE-VALUE` — a **version file** records a choice, so a complete version in one pins itself and a partial one is a prefix; a **command line** asks vibe to choose, so `SLOT@VER` stays a requirement. With that rule stated once, B-265 is the rule itself, B-262 is one more reader of it (`vibe install -g` with no version), B-263 is one more writer of the same spelling (`vibe app versions [PATTERN]`), and B-264 is the flag that makes the round trip closed (`vibe app env --write-version-file`). Had they been taken one at a time, each would have grown its own matcher. **(2) The prefix lowering is counting fields, and that is the whole implementation.** Three components → `=X.Y.Z`, two → `~X.Y`, one → `^X`, an optional leading `v` tolerated before a digit, and anything that is not a bare dotted run of digits (or a complete semver with a pre-release) left to the parser it already went through. One function in `vibe_app::versionfile::formats`, called by the search, the resolution cache's re-read of the authored value, and the listing's pattern — so a cache hit and a cold read cannot disagree, and a listing cannot narrow by a different rule than an activation selects by. A field that overflows `u64` is not a version prefix and keeps the ordinary meaning. **(3) B-262's chicken-and-egg was a false problem, measured.** The row feared that a package's declared version files are unknown until the package is resolved. They are not: the home's `vibe-app-version-files/1` sidecar records what every **installed** application declares, which is the same document an activation reads, so the install consults a file exactly when this home already has a provider of that slot. A first install of a package the home never held therefore resolves as it always did, and nothing resolves twice. **(4) B-264's open decision, taken: exactly one `--use`.** `vibe app env` resolves several slots in one call, so the flag names the slot by naming the version — one `--use SLOT=VER`, and the five other shapes are usage refusals naming the flag. The written path goes to **stderr**, because `app env`'s stdout is the only thing a shell evaluates; `--json` carries it as the one new optional member of `vibe-app-env/1`. **(5) The shim got smaller in three places, and that is the check that the features are the right ones.** `nvm install` with no version is now one `vibe install -g` with no version — the shim no longer reads the file's value through `app env --project` and re-translates it, which was version logic applied to a file vibe had already read. `nvm use --save` is one `vibe app env --use … --write-version-file`, so it no longer moves the slot default as a side effect nvm does not have. `nvm ls <pattern>` and `ls-remote <pattern>` hand the spelling to `vibe app versions` as the user typed it and list **every** match, where before each answered with the one version a requirement resolved to. What stayed is the `=<version>` translation of `#P7F-AS-BUILT` (1): a *target* is a requirement, and nothing about that changed. The shim is `org.vibevm.node/vibenvm@1.1.0`, and the differential verdict is **0** again over the same nine cases and all 52 required pairs. **(6) The whole-campaign acceptance is `campaigns/app-versions-2026-11/accept.sh`, thirteen legs, and PLAN §7's own count resolves as 9 + 4.** §7's scenario is nine legs (install at a channel; the listing; `app env`; the prompt hook; `app exec`; `app migrate`; the mirror from `mirror.toml`; the install from the snapshot with the network denied; the differential proof) and the owner's decisions of 2026-11-10 added four (a `keyed` file written and read back for two slots; the user's extras list reaching a new version; a recommendation declined with `--no-recommends`; an ordinary package's judged `slot:post-install` contribution and its unmet `needs`). All thirteen pass. It is network-isolated the way `campaigns/sys-prompt-2026-11/accept.sh` is — one re-exec into `bwrap --unshare-net`, every `vibe` call under `strace -e trace=connect`, any non-loopback `connect(2)` failing the run — and it reaches **no** upstream host: Node's release files come from the one documented mirror this repository pins, served over loopback and redirected by a `[[remap]]` row, which is the mechanism a closed network uses anyway. **(7) Two things the acceptance measured that the plan assumed, and they are recorded rather than asserted.** The "install from the snapshot with the network denied" leg needs the **bytes** as well as the manifest, so the mirror row sets `payloads = true` with `[payloads] into`, and the closed home reads them through an `[artifacts] packages` drop — the install's own plan says «1 input(s) from the [artifacts] packages drop», which is the proof that `#MIRROR-PAYLOAD-PROJECTION` and PROP-066 `#drops` meet. And PLAN §7 asks for the ordinary package's contributions in `--plan-only`: the ordinary plane's preview does **not** carry them, because PROP-065 `#ordinary-plan` is `impl/work` and `AV-FMT-032` was deliberately not delivered by P7e, so the leg measures the row in the install's own `contributions` array — where it exists, with its point, handler and outcome — and says so in its own comment instead of asserting a surface the campaign did not build.

p.CORP-PROOF-FIX-AS-BUILT: **Implemented 2026-11-11 — the three defects the corporate-network proof found in the shipped surface, and what closing them decided.** None was found by the differential suite, and saying why is the point of this record. **(1) `nvm use 22 --save` exited 0 and wrote nothing** — one `*) break` in the shim's option loop, which stopped parsing at the version and dropped every flag behind it. The audit the fix demanded went branch by branch against the pinned `nvm.sh` v0.41.0, and the discipline it found is `#VIBENVM-ARGUMENT-ORDER`: five different rules, one per branch, where the shim had one. Three further divergences came out of the same audit and are closed with it — `--reinstall-packages-from <v>` was accepted where nvm refuses the space spelling, a repeated `--save` was last-one-wins where nvm exits 6, and an unknown long option was ignored by `ls`, `ls-remote`, `version-remote` and `exec` where nvm refuses it. The suite missed all of them because **no case asked for a flag after the version**; one case now asks every wish in both positions. **(2) `nvm use default` exited 3** — `default` was handed to vibe as a requirement, where it is a channel nothing declares, though `#VIBENVM-MAPPING` already said it is the slot default. The spelling now resolves through the one translation table (`#VIBENVM-BUILT-IN-ALIASES`), so it works wherever a version does; the suite missed it because its cases reached `default` only through `install --default`, never by naming it. **(3) `nvm ls-remote --lts` answered `N/A` and exited 3**, and that one was not the shim at all: `vibe app versions <coordinate> --channel lts` refused with `unknown_channel … channels: (none)` while `--installed` showed the channels in the same home. The root cause is `#VERSIONS-CHANNEL-DISCOVERY` — the roots enumeration knew only `localdir`, so a home whose only registry is a mirrored `monorepo` discovered no template at all — and the suite **could not** have caught it: its sandbox B publishes into a `localdir` registry, so the registry type the corporate shape uses is structurally outside the suite's reach. That gap is closed where it can be measured instead: `crates/vibe-cli/tests/cli_app_versions_monorepo.rs` drives the listing over a real local `monorepo` registry with no `--registry` on the command line, and the corporate proof re-runs the three commands against `~/corp/admin/vibevm-repo` with the network denied. **(4) Fixing (3) uncovered a second defect inside it, and this is the one worth remembering.** Adding the monorepo root was not enough: a monorepo root is a `tempfile::TempDir` capture the registry **owns**, so the enumeration was handing back a path that the drop of its own resolver deleted before the caller read it — the channel table stayed empty and the version list stayed right, which is the same symptom as the first half. The roots now travel with their lease. A read-only enumeration that returns paths into something it opened must return the lease with them, and that is the general lesson, not a detail of monorepos.
